skills.objective: Students count a group of up to 20 objects with one number for each object, understand that the last number said tells how many, and see that the count stays the same when the objects move.
skills.studentObjective: I can count a group of things and tell how many there are.
skills.languageObjective: I will tell how many using the words count, how many and last number in the sentence 'There are ___.'
successCriteria: I touch or move each thing one time and say one number for each thing.
I say the last number and tell that it is how many.
I count again after the things are moved and get the same number.
I answer 'How many?' in a full sentence.
skills.bigIdea: The last number you say when you count tells how many, and moving the things around does not change how many there are.

syntax: There are ___ seeds.
The last number I said is ___.
discourse: Tell a partner how you counted

domains.listening: Students listen to a counting story and say the number that tells how many.
domains.speaking: Students count aloud with a partner and answer 'How many?' with 'There are ___.'
domains.reading: Students read a short counting story with number symbols and picture support.
domains.writing: Students write a number and a short sentence that tells how many.

vocab.def: To say numbers in order, one for each thing.
vocab.example: Lin counts 1, 2, 3 as she touches 3 seeds.
vocab.nonExample: Saying 1, 2, 3 fast without touching the seeds
vocab.sentence: I count the seeds one at a time.
vocab.everyday: To trust someone, as in 'You can count on me.'

vocab.def: A question that asks for the number of things.
vocab.example: How many seeds are in the row?
vocab.nonExample: What color are the seeds?
vocab.sentence: How many seeds does Lin have?

vocab.def: The last one you say when you count. It tells how many.
vocab.example: When you count 1 to 8, the last number is 8.
vocab.nonExample: The first number you say, which is 1
vocab.sentence: The last number I said is 8, so there are 8 seeds.

vocab.def: Things that are together in one set.
vocab.example: A group of 5 acorns on the table
vocab.nonExample: One acorn by itself
vocab.sentence: Tomás mixes the group of seeds.

vocab.def: A box with 2 rows of 5 spaces for counting.
vocab.example: A ten frame with 7 dots shows 5 in the top row and 2 in the bottom row.
vocab.nonExample: A long line of 10 dots with no rows
vocab.sentence: Lin puts 8 seeds in a ten frame.

misconceptions.belief: I can say numbers while I point anywhere, and the last number is still right.
misconceptions.why: Students say the number words faster than they touch objects, so some objects get two numbers and some get none.
misconceptions.fix: Slide each counted object to the side, or touch each one once, and say one number for each touch.

errorCase.story: Amara counts 6 stars in a row.
steps: Amara touches star 1 and says 1, star 2 and says 2, star 3 and says 3.
She touches star 3 again and says 4. Then she touches the last three stars and says 5, 6, 7.
The last number is 7, so Amara says there are 7 stars.
errorCase.explain: Each star gets one number and is counted only once. Touching star 3 twice made an extra number. There are 6 stars.

misconceptions.belief: If the things are spread out, there are more of them.
misconceptions.why: A longer line looks like more, and students trust what they see more than what they counted.
misconceptions.fix: Count the bears in a short pile, spread them out, and count again. Say 'Nothing was added, so it is still the same.'

errorCase.story: Kofi counts 5 bears in a short line. Then his friend spreads the bears far apart.
steps: Kofi counts the bears in the short line: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.
His friend spreads the bears apart so the line takes up more room.
Kofi says there are more bears now because the line is longer.
errorCase.explain: Spreading the bears out does not add any bears. Nothing was added or taken away, so there are still 5 bears.

misconceptions.belief: I can answer 'How many?' with a word like 'lots' or 'big'.
misconceptions.why: The phrase 'how many' is new, so students answer with a size word instead of a number.
misconceptions.fix: Always answer with a number and the frame 'There are ___.' Count first, then say the sentence.

misconceptions.belief: Fourteen is written 41 because I hear 'four' first.
misconceptions.why: In the spoken word fourteen the ones part comes first, but the written number puts the ten first.
misconceptions.fix: Build 14 with a ten frame and 4 more, then say 'one ten and four ones' and write the 1 first.

errorCase.story: Hana hears the number fourteen and writes it.
steps: Hana hears 'four' first and then 'teen'.
She writes the 4 first and then the 1.
She writes 41.
errorCase.explain: Fourteen is 1 ten and 4 ones, so the 1 is written first: 14. The number 41 is a different number.

reading.title: Lin Counts Bean Seeds
reading.text: Lin plants bean seeds in the school garden. She wants to know how many seeds she has. Lin puts the seeds in a row. She touches one seed at a time and says one number for each seed. She counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The last number is 8, so there are 8 seeds. Next Lin puts the seeds in a ten frame. The frame has 2 rows with 5 spaces in each row. The seeds fill the top row and 3 spaces in the bottom row. Her friend Tomás mixes the seeds into a new group. He asks, Are there more seeds now? Lin counts again and gets 8 again. Mixing the seeds does not change how many.
reading.simple: Lin has bean seeds. She wants to know how many. She touches each seed one time and says a number. She counts 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The last number is 8, so there are 8 seeds. Lin puts the seeds in a ten frame. The frame has 2 rows with 5 spaces in each row. The seeds fill 5 spaces and 3 more spaces. Tomás mixes the seeds up. Lin counts again. She still gets 8.

questions.q: How many seeds does Lin count?
Why does Lin count again after Tomás mixes the seeds?
questions.a: Tomás asks if there are more seeds, and counting again shows there are still 8.

questions.q: How many spaces in the bottom row of the ten frame have seeds?

wdntb.why: The hearts show 6 things. The other three groups show 5 things.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a ten frame with 7 dots. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If you count the same things in a different order, you get the same number.
asn.why: The number of things stays the same, so every order ends at the same last number.

asn.claim: If you spread the things out, there are more of them.
asn.why: Spreading out does not add anything, so the number stays the same.

wyr.q: Would you rather count 12 cubes in a row or 10 cubes in a ten frame and 2 more?

compare.a: Sofia moves each shoe to a new spot after she counts it.
compare.b: Omar leaves the shoes where they are and touches each one.
compare.prompt: Which way helps you count each shoe only one time? Explain.

debate.claim: The last number you say tells how many.
debate.forEvidence: Lin counts 1 to 8, and when she counts again she gets 8 again, so 8 is how many seeds there are.
debate.againstEvidence: The 8 is only the name of the last seed, so you have to count the group again to know how many.

listening.script: Listen to Tomás tell about the class fish tank. I count the orange fish first: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Then I count the white fish. There is 1. Now I count all the fish. I touch each fish one time and say 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The last number is 6, so there are 6 fish in the tank. Later the fish swim to the other side. My friend says there are more fish because they are far apart. I count again and I still get 6. Swimming does not add any fish.

tasks.q: How many fish are in the tank?
tasks.why: Tomás counts 5 orange fish and 1 white fish, and the last number he says is 6.

tasks.q: A friend says there are more fish because they swim far apart. What is the error?
options: Swimming apart does not add fish, so there are still 6.
The white fish should not be counted.
tasks.why: Nothing was added or taken away, so the number of fish is the same.

story.title: The Seed Count
story.goal: count every bean seed before planting day
story.intro: Lin has a pile of bean seeds and a ten frame, and the garden club needs to know how many seeds to plant.

beats.lead: Lin places the seeds in the ten frame one at a time.
beats.success: Lin touches each seed once, and her last number matches the seeds in the frame.
beats.redirect: Lin sees a seed she touched twice, so she slides each counted seed to the side and starts again.

beats.lead: Tomás brings a second bag and asks how many seeds are in the pile.
beats.success: Tomás hears the last number and knows that it tells how many.
beats.redirect: Tomás asks what the last number means, and Lin explains that it tells how many.

beats.lead: The garden club sorts the seeds into groups for each bed.
beats.success: Every bed gets a group, and Lin counts each group with care.
beats.redirect: One group looks bigger, so Lin counts it again and finds the same number.

story.ending: The seeds are counted, the beds are planted, and Lin can tell anyone how she knows how many.

panels.says: I count 7 acorns. I say 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7.
Let me spread the acorns out. Now there must be more!
Count them again and touch each acorn one time.

predict.q: Tomás pushes the 7 acorns into a tight pile. Before Lin counts, predict how many acorns there will be.
predict.why: Moving things closer or farther apart does not change how many.

transfer.relationship: One number for each thing, and the last number tells how many
phrasings: I count 8 seeds and the last number I say is 8
There are 8 seeds
A ten frame with 5 in the top row and 3 in the bottom row
8 is how many seeds are in the group

decoys.text: I count 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so there are 8 seeds
decoys.why: The last number said was 7, so there are 7 seeds.

decoys.text: The seeds are spread out, so there are more than 8 seeds
decoys.why: Spreading the seeds out does not change how many there are.

modeling.title: Counting garden supplies
modeling.scenario: A fictional garden club has some flower pots and some seed packets on a table, and the club wants to know if it has a pot for every packet.
assumptions: Every pot and every packet is counted one time.
All of the pots are whole and can be used.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: Count the pots and the packets. How many of each are there?
Does the club have a pot for every packet? Tell how you know.
How could you count the packets so that no packet is counted twice?
limits: A real club might have pots of different sizes, and counting does not tell the sizes.
Counting tells how many, but it does not tell if there is enough soil.

sentence.because: There are 8 seeds because the last number I said was 8.
sentence.but: The seeds are spread out, but there are still 8 seeds.
sentence.so: I touched each seed one time, so the last number tells how many.

diagnostic.prompt: Put 9 counters in a messy pile. Ask: How many counters are there? Show me how you know.
lookFor: Touches or moves each counter one time
Says one number for each counter in order
Names the last number as how many
diagnostic.language: If the student counts correctly with the hands but cannot say a full sentence, the barrier is language. Accept 'There are 9' with a finger pointing at the group.

extension.task: Count 14 counters in a line. Then show the same 14 counters in a ten frame with some extra. Show that both ways give the same number.
extension.reasoning: Tell a friend why spreading out or grouping the counters does not change how many.

en.learning: Your child is learning to count objects carefully and to know that the last number said tells how many.
en.say: Touch each thing one time and say one number for each thing.
en.ask: How many are there? How do you know?
en.activity: Count socks, spoons or stairs together. Move each thing as you count it, then count again in a different order.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a contar objetos con cuidado y a saber que el último número que se dice indica cuántos hay.
es.say: Toquen cada cosa una sola vez y digan un número para cada una.
es.activity: Cuenten calcetines, cucharas o escalones juntos. Muevan cada cosa mientras cuentan y luego vuelvan a contar en otro orden.

skills.objective: Students name the number that is one more or one less than a number within 100, and ten more or ten less than a multiple-of-ten or two-digit number, by reasoning about tens and ones.
skills.studentObjective: I can find one more, one less, ten more and ten less than a number.
skills.languageObjective: I will tell how a number changes using the words one more, one less and ten more in a sentence.
successCriteria: I name the number that is one more and the number that is one less.
I name the number that is ten more and the number that is ten less.
I tell which digit changed and which digit stayed the same.
I check my answer on a number line or a hundred chart.
skills.bigIdea: One more or one less changes the ones digit, and ten more or ten less changes the tens digit by 1.

syntax: ___ is one more than ___.
Ten more than ___ is ___ because the tens digit went up by 1.
discourse: Tell a partner which digit changed and why

domains.listening: Students listen to a ticket-collecting story and name the number after each change.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner a number, then say one more, one less and ten more.
domains.reading: Students read a short shelf story and underline each number and each change.
domains.writing: Students write a sentence that tells how a number changed and which digit moved.

vocab.def: The next number when you count up by 1.
vocab.example: One more than 46 is 47.
vocab.nonExample: 46 and 56, which are ten apart
vocab.sentence: Priya finds the book that is one more than 46.

vocab.def: The number just before. You count back by 1.
vocab.example: One less than 46 is 45.
vocab.nonExample: 36, which is ten less than 46
vocab.sentence: The book with one less than 46 is number 45.

vocab.def: Add 1 ten. The tens digit goes up by 1.
vocab.example: Ten more than 46 is 56.
vocab.nonExample: 47, which is only one more than 46
vocab.sentence: Samir finds ten more than 46 by moving down one row.

vocab.def: A line with numbers in order, like a ruler.
vocab.example: A line that shows 30, 31, 32 up to 40
vocab.nonExample: A list of numbers in a mixed-up order
vocab.sentence: They draw a number line to check their hops.

vocab.def: One of the symbols 0 to 9 used to write numbers.
vocab.example: The number 46 has two digits: 4 and 6.
vocab.nonExample: The word forty-six
vocab.sentence: Only the tens digit changed from 46 to 56.

misconceptions.belief: Ten more means the ones digit goes up by 1.
misconceptions.why: Students know that adding changes the last digit, so they change the ones digit even when the amount is a ten.
misconceptions.fix: Build the number with tens and ones blocks, add 1 ten stick, and watch which digit changes.

errorCase.story: Omar has 34 stickers and gets ten more stickers.
steps: Omar starts with 34 stickers, which is 3 tens and 4 ones.
Ten more means add 1 to the number, so he writes 35.
Omar says he has 35 stickers.
errorCase.explain: Ten more changes the tens digit, not the ones digit. 3 tens and 1 more ten is 4 tens, so ten more than 34 is 44.

misconceptions.belief: When I count back, the number I start on is the first step.
misconceptions.why: Students say the starting number out loud as they count back, so they count it as a step.
misconceptions.fix: Put a finger on the start and say nothing. The first number you say after the finger moves is one less.

errorCase.story: Zara wants one less than 40.
steps: Zara starts at 40 and counts back.
She says 40, 39, 38 and stops at 38 because she counted 40 as her first step.
She says one less than 40 is 38.
errorCase.explain: The starting number is not a step. One step back from 40 lands on 39, so one less than 40 is 39.

misconceptions.belief: 'One less than 12' means 12 is the answer.
misconceptions.why: In the phrase 'one less than 12' the starting number comes last, so students grab the number they hear first or last.
misconceptions.fix: Say it as a small story: start at 12, go back 1. Use a number line and point to the start first.

misconceptions.belief: A tens digit cannot go past 9, so ten more than 90 is 910.
misconceptions.why: Students treat each digit as a separate counter and write a new digit after the 9.
misconceptions.fix: Count by tens with blocks: 80, 90, then 10 tens. Show that 10 tens trade for 1 hundred.

errorCase.story: Jabari has 90 pennies and gets ten more pennies.
steps: Jabari has 9 tens and 0 ones.
He adds 1 ten and writes the new ten after the 9 to get 910.
He says ten more than 90 is 910.
errorCase.explain: 9 tens and 1 more ten make 10 tens, and 10 tens are 100. Ten more than 90 is 100.

reading.title: The Number Shelf
reading.text: Priya and her brother Samir help in the school library. The books on one shelf have number stickers. Priya holds a book with the number 46. She finds the book that is one more. It is 47. Then she finds one less. It is 45. Samir wants ten more than 46. He walks down one whole row of ten books. The book there is 56. Priya sees that 46 and 56 have the same ones digit. Only the tens digit changed. Samir says ten less than 46 is 36. They draw a number line to check. They hop 1 forward for one more and 1 back for one less. Then they hop 10 for ten more.
reading.simple: Priya and Samir help in the library. Priya has a book with the number 46. One more is 47. One less is 45. Samir finds ten more than 46. It is 56. Only the tens digit changed. Ten less than 46 is 36. They draw a number line. They hop 1 forward and 1 back. Then they hop 10 for ten more.

questions.q: What number is one more than 46?
Why does only the tens digit change when Samir finds ten more?
questions.a: Ten more adds 1 ten, so the tens digit goes up by 1 and the ones stay the same.

questions.q: What is ten less than 46?

wdntb.why: 56 has 5 tens, and the other three numbers have 4 tens.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the numbers 23, 33, 43 and 53. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: When you find ten more than a number up to 90, the ones digit stays the same.
asn.why: Ten more adds only a ten, so the ones do not change.

asn.claim: One more than a number is smaller than the number.
asn.why: One more is the next number when you count up, so it is greater.

wyr.q: Would you rather find ten more on a hundred chart or on a number line?

compare.a: Nia adds 1 to the tens digit of 52 and writes 62.
compare.b: Leo adds 1 to the ones digit of 52 and writes 53.
compare.prompt: Who found ten more than 52? Who found one more? How do you know?

debate.claim: It is easier to find ten more by changing the tens digit than by counting up 10 times.
debate.forEvidence: Changing the tens digit takes one step. The tens digit in 46 goes from 4 to 5, and you have 56 right away.
debate.againstEvidence: Counting up 10 times shows every number between 46 and 56, so you can check that you did not skip any.

listening.script: Listen to Kofi talk about his bus tickets. I have 38 tickets. My sister gives me one more. Now I have 39. Then I give one ticket to a friend, so I have one less and I am back at 38. Then my aunt gives me a pack of ten tickets. Ten more than 38 is 48. The tens digit went from 3 to 4, and the ones digit is still 8. A friend says the ones digit changes when you add ten. But that is not what happened to my tickets.

tasks.q: How many tickets does Kofi have after his aunt gives him a pack of ten?
tasks.why: Ten more than 38 is 48, because the tens digit goes from 3 to 4.

tasks.q: A friend says the ones digit changes when you add ten. What is the error?
options: Adding ten changes the tens digit and the ones digit stays the same.
Adding ten makes the number smaller.
The ones digit is the first digit.
tasks.why: Kofi's number went from 38 to 48, so only the tens digit changed.

story.title: The Shelf Cart
story.goal: put each numbered book in the right spot on the shelves
story.intro: Zara pushes a cart of books with number stickers, and each shelf card asks for the book that is one more, one less or ten more.

beats.lead: Zara reads the first shelf card and looks for the book that is one more.
beats.success: Zara picks the next number in counting order, and the book fits the shelf.
beats.redirect: The book is ten away, not one away, so Zara counts up one step from the start and tries again.

beats.lead: A second card asks for the book that is ten less.
beats.success: Zara changes the tens digit down by 1, and the ones digit stays put.
beats.redirect: The ones digit changed by mistake, so Zara builds the number with tens sticks and takes away one stick.

beats.lead: The last card asks Zara to explain her choices to the librarian.
beats.success: Zara says which digit moved for each book and why.
beats.redirect: Zara's explanation skips a step, so she points to the number line and tells it again.

story.ending: Every book sits in the right place, and Zara can show how one step and ten steps change a number.

panels.says: My card says 63. I need the card that is ten more.
I will add 1 to the ones digit and write 64.
That is one more. Ten more is one whole row down on the hundred chart.
Oh! The tens digit goes from 6 to 7, so ten more than 63 is 73.

predict.q: Omar now wants ten less than 63. Before Zara answers, predict the number.
predict.why: Ten less takes away 1 ten, so the tens digit goes from 6 to 5 and the ones digit stays 3.

transfer.relationship: Ten more or ten less changes the tens digit by 1 and keeps the ones digit
phrasings: Ten more than 63 is 73
On a hundred chart, 73 is one row below 63
6 tens and 3 ones becomes 7 tens and 3 ones
Add 1 ten to 63

decoys.why: 64 is one more than 63, not ten more.
53 is ten less than 63, so the tens digit went the wrong way.

modeling.title: Numbering the library shelves
modeling.scenario: A fictional library puts a number sticker on every shelf. The shelves are numbered in counting order, and a helper starts with a cart at shelf 27.
assumptions: The shelves are numbered in counting order with none missing.
Each row has exactly 10 shelves.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: What shelf number is one more than 27? What shelf number is one less?
The helper walks down 1 row of ten shelves from shelf 27. Which shelf is that?
What shelf would the helper reach by walking back 1 row from shelf 27?
limits: Real libraries often label shelves with letters and other symbols, not only counting numbers.
A shelf row may not hold exactly 10 shelves in a real building.

sentence.because: 46 is one more than 45 because 46 comes right after 45 when we count.
sentence.but: 46 and 56 look almost the same, but 56 is ten more.
sentence.so: The tens digit went up by 1, so the number is ten more.

diagnostic.prompt: Ask: What is one more than 58? One less than 58? Ten more than 58? Ten less than 58? Let the student use a number line or a hundred chart.
lookFor: Changes the ones digit by 1 for one more and one less
Changes the tens digit by 1 for ten more and ten less
Names which digit stayed the same
diagnostic.language: If the student points to the right number on the hundred chart but cannot say it, the barrier is language. Offer the frame: ___ is ten more than ___.

extension.task: Start at 24. Make a path of three hops using one more, one less and ten more in any order. Where do you land?
extension.reasoning: Explain why you land on the same number when you change the order of the hops.

en.learning: Your child is learning to find the number that is one more, one less, ten more or ten less than a number up to 100.
en.say: When you add ten, look at the tens digit. It goes up by 1.
en.ask: What is ten more than 35? What is one less than 35?
en.activity: Use the stairs, a calendar or a hundred chart. Pick a number and take turns saying one more, one less or ten more.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a encontrar el número que es uno más, uno menos, diez más o diez menos que un número hasta el 100.
es.say: Cuando sumen diez, miren el dígito de las decenas. Sube 1.
es.ask: ¿Cuánto es diez más que 35? ¿Cuánto es uno menos que 35?
es.activity: Usen las escaleras, un calendario o una tabla de cien. Elijan un número y túrnense para decir uno más, uno menos o diez más.

skills.objective: Students add and subtract within 20 by joining and separating groups, using number bonds and counting on, and they see that addition and subtraction use the same parts and total.
skills.studentObjective: I can add and subtract numbers up to 20 and show how I know.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain how parts and a total fit together using the words add, subtract, part and total.
successCriteria: I add two numbers within 20 and say the total.
I subtract a part from a total within 20 and say what is left.
I show the parts and the total in a number bond.
I check that the total is bigger than each part.
skills.bigIdea: Two parts make a total, and when you take one part away from the total, the other part is left.

syntax: ___ and ___ make a total of ___.
The total is ___ and one part is ___, so the other part is ___.
discourse: Explain to a partner how you found the total or the missing part

domains.listening: Students listen to a bead-box description and name the total and the part that is left.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they added or subtracted, using part and total words.
domains.reading: Students read a short bracelet story and circle each part and the total.
domains.writing: Students write an addition or subtraction sentence and a sentence about the total.

vocab.def: To join two groups and find the total.
vocab.example: Add 8 red beads and 5 blue beads to get 13 beads.
vocab.nonExample: Taking 5 beads away from 13 beads
vocab.sentence: Mei will add her red beads and her blue beads.

vocab.def: To take away some and find how many are left.
vocab.example: Subtract 6 from 15 to find that 9 are left.
vocab.nonExample: Joining 6 more beads to 15 beads
vocab.sentence: Diego will subtract the beads he gave away.

vocab.def: One of the smaller groups that make a bigger group.
vocab.example: In 8 + 5 = 13, the numbers 8 and 5 are parts.
vocab.nonExample: 13, which is the whole group
vocab.sentence: The other part is 9, because 9 + 6 = 15.
vocab.everyday: A piece of something, or a role in a play, like a part in the class show.

vocab.def: How many there are when all the parts are put together.
vocab.example: The total of 8 and 5 is 13.
vocab.nonExample: One part by itself, like 8
vocab.sentence: The total is 13 beads.

vocab.def: A picture that shows two parts and the total.
vocab.example: A bond with 12 on top and 7 and 5 below
vocab.nonExample: A list of numbers with no total
vocab.sentence: Diego draws a number bond with 15 as the total.

misconceptions.belief: When I count on, the number I start on is the first count.
misconceptions.why: Students say the starting number out loud with the first finger, so the count is one short.
misconceptions.fix: Say the start number, then put up a finger for each number after it: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 for 5 fingers.

errorCase.story: Tomás adds 8 + 5 by counting on.
steps: He says 8 and holds up 5 fingers.
He says 8 for the first finger, then 9, 10, 11 and 12 for the other fingers.
He says 8 + 5 = 12.
errorCase.explain: The starting number is not counted again. Say 9, 10, 11, 12, 13 for the 5 fingers, so 8 + 5 = 13.

misconceptions.belief: In subtraction I can swap the numbers, like in addition.
misconceptions.why: Students learn that 3 + 5 and 5 + 3 match, and they expect every operation to work that way.
misconceptions.fix: Act it out: start with the total, take away a part. Show that you cannot take 12 beads from 4 beads.

errorCase.story: Yuki has 12 beads and gives 4 beads to a friend.
steps: Yuki starts with 12 beads.
She writes 4 − 12 = 8 because she says the order does not matter.
She says she has 8 beads left.
errorCase.explain: In subtraction the total goes first, then the part that is taken away. She starts with 12 and takes away 4, so 12 − 4 = 8.

misconceptions.belief: The minus sign means add, because both signs are short lines.
misconceptions.why: The signs + and − look alike at a quick glance, so students read them as the same sign.
misconceptions.fix: Trace each sign with a finger and say its job: plus joins, minus takes away. Use counters to match.

misconceptions.belief: The biggest number in a number bond can be one of the parts.
misconceptions.why: Students do not yet see that the total must be at least as big as each part.
misconceptions.fix: Put counters in two cups and then pour them into one big cup. The big cup always holds the most.

errorCase.story: Ana has a number bond where the total is 12 and one part is 7.
steps: The total is 12 and one part is 7.
To find the other part she adds 12 + 7.
12 + 7 = 19, so the other part is 19.
errorCase.explain: The two parts must make the total of 12, so the other part is smaller than 12. Subtract: 12 − 7 = 5. The other part is 5.

reading.title: Bracelet Beads
reading.text: Mei and Diego make bracelets in art class. Mei has 8 red beads and 5 blue beads. She wants to add them to find the total. She holds 8 in her head and counts on 5 more: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. The total is 13 beads. Diego has 15 beads. He gives 6 beads to a friend, so he must subtract. He draws a number bond with 15 as the total and 6 as one part. The other part is 9, because 9 + 6 = 15. Diego has 9 beads left. Mei says each part and the total can make two addition facts and two subtraction facts.
reading.simple: Mei and Diego make bracelets. Mei has 8 red beads and 5 blue beads. She wants to add to find the total. She counts on 5 more: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. The total is 13 beads. Diego has 15 beads. He gives 6 beads away, so he must subtract. He draws a number bond. The total is 15 and one part is 6. The other part is 9. Diego has 9 beads left.

questions.q: How many red beads does Mei have?
Why does Diego use 15 as the total in his number bond?
questions.a: He started with 15 beads, and the parts 6 and 9 make 15.

questions.q: What is 15 − 6?

wdntb.why: 8 + 5, 9 + 4 and 10 + 3 all equal 13. 15 − 3 is a subtraction and equals 12.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at 8 + 5 = 13, 9 + 4 = 13 and 10 + 3 = 13. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: If you know 6 + 7 = 13, then you know 13 − 7 = 6.
asn.why: The parts 6 and 7 make the total 13, so taking one part from the total leaves the other part.

asn.claim: When you subtract, the answer is bigger than the number you start with.
asn.why: Taking some away leaves fewer than you started with.

wyr.q: Would you rather add 9 + 6 by counting on or by using a number bond?

compare.a: Diego solves 14 − 5 by counting back 5 from 14.
compare.b: Mei solves 14 − 5 by asking what number goes with 5 to make 14.
compare.prompt: Do both ways find 14 − 5? Explain how each way works.

debate.claim: Counting on is the best way to add.
debate.forEvidence: Counting on from 8 for 5 more is quick: 9, 10, 11, 12, 13.
debate.againstEvidence: Counting on can slip by one, but a number bond uses facts you already know.

listening.script: Listen to Samir tell about his bead box. I have 7 green beads and 6 yellow beads. I want the total. I think 7 and 3 more make 10, then 3 more make 13. So I have 13 beads. Then I give 4 beads to my friend. I take 4 away and I have 9 beads left. My cousin says 13 minus 4 is 17. But 17 is more than 13, so that cannot be right. When I take beads away, I have fewer beads.

tasks.q: How many beads does Samir have after he gives 4 to his friend?
tasks.why: Samir has 13 beads and takes away 4, so 9 beads are left.

tasks.q: Samir's cousin says 13 minus 4 is 17. What is the error?
options: The cousin added instead of taking away.
tasks.why: Taking away makes fewer beads, so the answer must be less than 13.

story.title: The Bracelet Rush
story.goal: get the bracelets ready for the school fair
story.intro: Yuki is making bracelets for the school fair, and she keeps red beads in one cup and blue beads in another cup.

beats.lead: Yuki joins the beads from the two cups to see how many she has.
beats.success: Yuki joins the parts and finds the total, and her bracelet plan works.
beats.redirect: Yuki's total looks too small, so she checks that the total is bigger than each part.

beats.lead: A friend asks for some beads, so Yuki takes some away.
beats.success: Yuki subtracts and counts what is left, and the number makes sense.
beats.redirect: Yuki's answer is bigger than what she started with, so she checks whether she added by mistake.

beats.lead: The fair needs a poster that shows the parts and the total.
beats.success: The poster shows two parts that make the total, and every fact matches.
beats.redirect: One fact on the poster does not match the bond, so Yuki checks the parts again.

story.ending: The bracelets sell out, and Yuki can show with a number bond how the parts make the total.

panels.says: I have 9 beads and 4 more beads, and I counted on from 9.
How do you know your total is right?
I said 10, 11, 12, 13 for the 4 more beads, so 9 + 4 = 13.
Now take away 4. The number bond has 13 as the total, so I subtract.

predict.q: Ravi takes 4 beads away from the 13 beads. Before he says it, predict how many beads are left.
predict.why: 13 − 4 = 9, and the parts 9 and 4 make the total 13.

transfer.relationship: Two parts make a total, and the total take away one part leaves the other part
phrasings: A number bond with a total of 13 and parts 9 and 4
4 and what number make 13?

decoys.why: The total is the biggest number, so it cannot be the answer to an addition of 13 and 4.
Taking 4 away from 9 leaves less than 9, not 13.

modeling.title: Planning bracelet beads
modeling.scenario: A fictional art club has some beads and wants to make 2 bracelets. A shop gives the club some extra beads.
assumptions: Every bracelet uses exactly the same number of beads.
No bead is lost or broken.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: How many beads does the club have after the shop gives 5 more?
Is that enough for 2 bracelets that use 8 beads each? Show how you know.
How many beads are left after both bracelets are made?
limits: Real beads come in different sizes, so a bracelet may not use exactly 8.
We did not count the string or the clasp.

sentence.because: 9 + 4 = 13 because the parts 9 and 4 make the total 13.
sentence.but: 13 − 4 looks different from 9 + 4, but they use the same three numbers.
sentence.so: The total is 13 and one part is 4, so the other part is 9.

diagnostic.prompt: Give the student 8 counters and 6 counters. Ask: How many counters are there together? Then take away 5 from the total and ask: How many are left?
lookFor: Counts on without counting the first group again
Says the total is bigger than each part
Names what is left after taking away
diagnostic.language: If the student moves the counters correctly but cannot say add, subtract or total, the barrier is language. Let the student show the answer first, then give the word.

extension.task: Write 4 different addition or subtraction facts that use only the numbers 7, 8 and 15.
extension.reasoning: Explain how one number bond can give you all four facts.

en.learning: Your child is learning to add and subtract numbers up to 20 and to see how two parts and a total go together.
en.say: Two parts make a total. If you take one part away, the other part is left.
en.ask: We have 9 grapes and eat 4. How many are left? How did you find it?
en.activity: Put 12 small objects in two groups. Say the parts and the total, then write one adding and one subtracting sentence.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a sumar y restar números hasta el 20 y a ver cómo se relacionan dos partes y el total.
es.say: Dos partes forman el total. Si quitan una parte, queda la otra parte.
es.ask: Tenemos 9 uvas y nos comemos 4. ¿Cuántas quedan? ¿Cómo lo encontraste?
es.activity: Pongan 12 objetos pequeños en dos grupos. Digan las partes y el total, y luego escriban una suma y una resta.

skills.objective: Students understand that a two-digit number is made of tens and ones, read and write numbers up to 99, and see that 10 ones can be traded for 1 ten.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell how many tens and ones are in a two-digit number.
skills.languageObjective: I will say and write how many tens and ones a number has using the words tens, ones and place.
successCriteria: I say how many tens and how many ones are in a number up to 99.
I write the number that matches a group of tens and ones.
I trade 10 ones for 1 ten and say why the amount stays the same.
I tell what each digit means by its place.
skills.bigIdea: A digit means different amounts in different places: the digit on the left counts tens and the digit on the right counts ones.

syntax: The number ___ has ___ tens and ___ ones.
The digit ___ is in the tens place, so it means ___.
discourse: Tell a partner how you know which digit is in which place

domains.listening: Students listen to a pencil-pack story and say the number of tens and ones they hear.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how many tens and ones are in a number, and trade ones for a ten.
domains.reading: Students read a short store story and match each digit to its place.
domains.writing: Students write a number and a sentence that names its tens and ones.

vocab.def: Groups of 10 ones. A pack of 10 is 1 ten.
vocab.example: 3 packs of 10 pencils is 3 tens.
vocab.nonExample: 3 loose pencils, which are 3 ones
vocab.sentence: Aisha has 3 tens in the number 34.

vocab.def: Single things. 10 ones make 1 ten.
vocab.example: 4 loose pencils is 4 ones.
vocab.nonExample: A pack of 10 pencils
vocab.sentence: Aisha has 4 ones in the number 34.

vocab.def: A symbol from 0 to 9 used to write numbers.
vocab.example: The number 34 is written with the digits 3 and 4.
vocab.nonExample: The number 34 as a whole
vocab.sentence: The first digit in 34 shows the tens.

vocab.def: Where a digit sits in a number.
vocab.example: In 34, the 3 is in the tens place.
vocab.nonExample: The size of the digit
vocab.sentence: The place of a digit tells what it is worth.
vocab.everyday: A spot or a location, like a place to sit.

vocab.def: A number from 13 to 19. It has 1 ten and some ones.
vocab.example: 16 is 1 ten and 6 ones.
vocab.nonExample: 24, which has 2 tens
vocab.sentence: A teen number such as 16 has 1 ten.

misconceptions.belief: In 52, the 5 means five and the 2 means two, so the number means 5 + 2.
misconceptions.why: Students read each digit by itself and do not yet see that its place changes what it is worth.
misconceptions.fix: Build 52 with 5 ten sticks and 2 loose cubes, and say 'five tens, two ones' before writing the number.

errorCase.story: Lin has 5 packs of ten pencils and 2 loose pencils.
steps: Lin has 5 tens and 2 ones.
She says the 5 in 52 means 5 pencils.
She says there are 5 + 2 = 7 pencils.
errorCase.explain: The 5 in 52 means 5 tens, which is 50 pencils. 50 + 2 = 52, so there are 52 pencils, not 7.

misconceptions.belief: 1 ten is a smaller amount than 10 ones, because 1 is less than 10.
misconceptions.why: Students compare the numerals 1 and 10 and forget that a ten is a group of ten things.
misconceptions.fix: Snap 10 single cubes into one ten stick and count both. Say 'one ten is ten ones.'

errorCase.story: Omar has 10 loose cubes, and his friend has 1 stick of ten cubes.
steps: Omar has 10 ones.
His friend has 1 ten.
Omar says his friend has fewer cubes because 1 is less than 10.
errorCase.explain: 1 ten is a group of 10 cubes. It is the same amount as 10 ones, so both friends have 10 cubes.

misconceptions.belief: Twenty-seven is written 207, because I write 20 and then 7.
misconceptions.why: Students write each spoken part as its own number and put them side by side.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'two tens and seven ones' and write the 2 in the tens place and the 7 in the ones place.

errorCase.story: Aisha hears the number twenty-seven and writes it.
steps: Aisha hears 'twenty' and then 'seven'.
She writes 20 and then writes 7 next to it.
She writes 207.
errorCase.explain: Twenty-seven is 2 tens and 7 ones. The 7 fills the ones place, so the number is 27.

misconceptions.belief: '4 tens' and 4 mean the same amount.
misconceptions.why: The plural word tens names the size of the groups, but students hear only the count of 4.
misconceptions.fix: Build 4 packs of ten, count by tens to 40, and say '4 tens is 40.'

reading.title: Pencil Packs
reading.text: Aisha helps at the school store. The store sells pencils in packs of 10. A pack is 1 ten. Aisha has 3 packs and 4 loose pencils. She writes 3 tens and 4 ones. The digit 3 is in the tens place, and the digit 4 is in the ones place, so the number is 34. Her friend Jabari has 2 packs and 14 loose pencils. He says he has 2 tens and 14 ones. Aisha helps him trade 10 ones for 1 ten. Now Jabari has 3 tens and 4 ones. Both friends have the same number of pencils: 34.
reading.simple: Aisha helps at the school store. Pencils come in packs of 10. A pack is 1 ten. Aisha has 3 packs and 4 loose pencils. That is 3 tens and 4 ones. The number is 34. Jabari has 2 packs and 14 loose pencils. Aisha helps him trade 10 ones for 1 ten. Now Jabari has 3 tens and 4 ones. Both friends have 34 pencils.

questions.q: How many loose pencils does Aisha have?
Why do Aisha and Jabari have the same number of pencils?
questions.a: Jabari trades 10 ones for 1 ten, and then he also has 3 tens and 4 ones.

questions.q: What number is 3 tens and 4 ones?

wdntb.why: The first three all show 34. The number 43 is 4 tens and 3 ones.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at the numbers 20, 21, 22 and 23. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: You can show the same number with tens and ones in more than one way.
asn.why: 10 ones can be traded for 1 ten, so 2 tens and 15 ones show the same number as 3 tens and 5 ones.

asn.claim: The digit on the left in a two-digit number is the ones digit.
asn.why: The digit on the left is in the tens place, and the digit on the right is in the ones place.

wyr.q: Would you rather show 46 with blocks or with a drawing of tens and ones?

compare.a: Omar shows 35 as 3 tens and 5 ones.
compare.b: Nia shows 35 as 2 tens and 15 ones.
compare.prompt: Do both children show 35? Explain how you know.

debate.claim: Counting by tens is better than counting by ones.
debate.forEvidence: To count 40 pencils in packs of 10, you say 10, 20, 30, 40. That is only 4 numbers instead of 40.
debate.againstEvidence: Counting by ones works for any group, even when there are no full packs of ten.

listening.script: Listen to Kofi count pencils for his class. I have 4 packs of ten and 7 loose pencils. 4 tens is 40. I add the 7 ones. The number is 47. My friend writes 74. But 74 means 7 tens and 4 ones, and that is many more pencils than I have. In my number the digit 4 is in the tens place, and the digit 7 is in the ones place. The place of the digit tells what it is worth.

tasks.q: How many pencils does Kofi have?
tasks.why: Kofi has 4 tens and 7 ones, which is 40 and 7 more, or 47.

tasks.q: Kofi's friend writes 74. What is the error?
options: The friend put the tens digit and the ones digit in the wrong places.
The friend forgot to count the packs.
tasks.why: 74 is 7 tens and 4 ones, but Kofi has 4 tens and 7 ones.

story.title: Packs of Ten
story.goal: bundle loose pencils into packs of ten
story.intro: Sofia finds a big box of loose pencils in the storeroom, and the store sells them in packs of 10.

beats.lead: Sofia bundles ten pencils with a rubber band.
beats.success: Sofia makes one new ten, and the pile of loose pencils gets smaller.
beats.redirect: The bundle has too few pencils, so Sofia counts the ones in it until there are ten.

beats.lead: She sets bundles on one tray and loose pencils on another tray.
beats.success: The tray labels say tens and ones, and every pencil is in the right place.
beats.redirect: A bundle sits on the ones tray, so Sofia moves it to the tens tray.

beats.lead: A customer asks Sofia how many pencils she has in all.
beats.success: Sofia says the tens and the ones, and then she says the whole number.
beats.redirect: Sofia's number does not match the trays, so she checks which digit is in the tens place.

story.ending: The storeroom is neat, the packs are ready, and Sofia can say what every digit in the number means.

panels.says: I have 5 packs of ten and 3 loose pencils.
Is that 8 pencils? 5 and 3 make 8.
No, each pack is a ten. 5 tens is 50.
So 50 and 3 make 53 pencils. The 5 is in the tens place!

predict.q: Sofia gets 1 more pack, so she has 6 packs of ten and 3 loose pencils. Predict the number of pencils.
predict.why: 6 packs of ten is 60, and 3 loose pencils make 63.

transfer.relationship: A two-digit number is made of tens and ones
phrasings: 4 tens and 7 ones
4 packs of ten and 7 single pencils

decoys.why: The 4 means 4 tens, not 4 ones, so the number is 47.
This is 74. The tens and the ones are switched.

modeling.title: Packing the pencil order
modeling.scenario: A fictional school store gets a box of pencils for the new year. Pencils are sold in packs of 10, and any extras are sold one at a time.
assumptions: Every pack has exactly 10 pencils.
No pencil is broken or lost.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: How many full packs can the store make? How many pencils are left over?
A class buys 4 packs. How many pencils is that?
How many packs does the store have left after the class buys 4 packs?
limits: A real store might sell packs of other sizes.
The tens and ones model does not tell us how much each pencil costs.

sentence.base: The number 34 has 3 tens and 4 ones.
sentence.because: The number 34 has 3 tens because the digit 3 is in the tens place.
sentence.but: The digits 3 and 4 are in both 34 and 43, but the numbers are different.
sentence.so: The 3 is in the tens place, so it means 30.

diagnostic.prompt: Show 4 bundles of ten sticks and 6 loose sticks. Ask: How many sticks are there? Write the number and tell me what each digit means.
lookFor: Counts the bundles as tens and the loose sticks as ones
Writes the tens digit first and the ones digit second
Explains that the 4 means 4 tens
diagnostic.language: If the student counts the bundles and sticks correctly but swaps the words tens and ones, the barrier is language. Give two labeled trays and let the student point first.

extension.task: Show 52 in three ways: with tens and ones blocks, with a drawing and with an addition sentence. Then show 52 with only 4 tens and some ones.
extension.reasoning: Explain why 4 tens and 12 ones is still the number 52.

en.learning: Your child is learning that a two-digit number is made of tens and ones, like 34 is 3 tens and 4 ones.
en.say: The first digit tells how many tens. The second digit tells how many ones.
en.ask: How many tens and ones are in 47? How do you know?
en.activity: Bundle 10 spoons or crayons with a rubber band. Make a number such as 23 with bundles and singles and write it.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que un número de dos dígitos se forma con decenas y unidades, por ejemplo, 34 es 3 decenas y 4 unidades.
es.say: El primer dígito dice cuántas decenas hay. El segundo dígito dice cuántas unidades hay.
es.ask: ¿Cuántas decenas y unidades hay en 47? ¿Cómo lo sabes?
es.activity: Amarren 10 cucharas o crayones con una liga. Formen un número, como 23, con paquetes y piezas sueltas, y escríbanlo.

skills.objective: Students compare two two-digit numbers by reasoning about tens and then ones, and record the result with the symbols >, < and = and with a full sentence.
skills.studentObjective: I can compare two numbers and tell which is greater, which is less, or if they are equal.
skills.languageObjective: I will compare numbers using the words greater than, less than and equal to, and I will explain with the tens digit.
successCriteria: I look at the tens first and then the ones when I compare two numbers.
I say which number is greater and which is less.
I write the comparison with >, < or = so it matches what I said.
I explain my choice in a full sentence.
skills.bigIdea: To compare two-digit numbers, compare the tens first because a ten is worth more than any number of ones that fit in the ones place.

syntax: ___ is greater than ___ because it has more tens.
___ is less than ___.
discourse: Tell a partner which number is greater and defend your choice

domains.listening: Students listen to a comparison story and decide which number the speaker says is greater.
domains.speaking: Students say a comparison sentence and give a reason about tens and ones.
domains.reading: Students read a short shelter story and find each comparison sentence and symbol.
domains.writing: Students write a comparison with a symbol and a sentence that gives a reason.

vocab.def: To tell which number is bigger, smaller or the same.
vocab.example: Compare 47 and 52 to see which is greater.
vocab.nonExample: Counting the treats without checking another number
vocab.sentence: Hana and Ravi compare the two jars of treats.

vocab.def: Bigger than another number. Written with the sign >.
vocab.example: 52 is greater than 47, so 52 > 47.
vocab.nonExample: 47, which is less than 52
vocab.sentence: 52 is greater than 47 because it has more tens.

vocab.def: Smaller than another number. Written with the sign <.
vocab.example: 47 is less than 52, so 47 < 52.
vocab.nonExample: 52, which is greater than 47
vocab.sentence: The number 47 is less than 52.

vocab.def: The same amount as another number. Written with the sign =.
vocab.example: 52 is equal to 52, so 52 = 52.
vocab.nonExample: 47 and 52, which are different amounts
vocab.sentence: The two jars with 52 treats are equal to each other.

vocab.def: The digit that tells how many tens are in a number.
vocab.example: The tens digit of 47 is 4.
vocab.nonExample: The 7 in 47, which is the ones digit
vocab.sentence: Hana looks at the tens digit first.

misconceptions.belief: To compare two numbers, I look at the ones digits first.
misconceptions.why: Students read the digits from the right, or they notice the biggest single digit and trust it.
misconceptions.fix: Build both numbers with tens sticks and cubes. Line up the tens and ask which number has more sticks.

errorCase.story: Leo compares 38 and 52.
steps: 38 has 3 tens and 8 ones. 52 has 5 tens and 2 ones.
Leo compares the ones first. 8 is greater than 2.
So Leo says 38 is greater than 52.
errorCase.explain: Compare the tens first. 5 tens is more than 3 tens, so 52 is greater than 38.

misconceptions.belief: The pointy end of the symbol goes next to the greater number.
misconceptions.why: Students notice that the symbol opens wide and closes to a point, and they match the wrong end to the bigger number.
misconceptions.fix: Read the symbol as a sentence, left to right, and check it with the words greater than or less than.

errorCase.story: Nia compares 61 and 59 with a symbol.
steps: 61 has 6 tens and 59 has 5 tens.
6 tens is more than 5 tens, so 61 is greater than 59.
Nia writes 61 < 59 because she thinks the pointy end goes next to the greater number.
errorCase.explain: The pointy end goes next to the smaller number, and the open side faces the greater number. The right way is 61 > 59, or 59 < 61.

misconceptions.belief: '38 is less than 52' means 52 is the number that is less.
misconceptions.why: In the sentence the greater number comes last, and students attach 'less' to the number they hear last.
misconceptions.fix: Say the sentence about the first number: 38 is less, so it comes first. Use a number line to see which one is farther left.

misconceptions.belief: 9 is greater than 10 because 9 is a big digit.
misconceptions.why: Students compare single digits and forget that 10 means 1 ten, which is more than 9 ones.
misconceptions.fix: Show 9 cubes next to a ten stick and ask which has more.

errorCase.story: Zara compares 9 and 10.
steps: 9 has one digit and 10 has two digits.
Zara says 9 is bigger than the 1 and the 0.
She says 9 is greater than 10.
errorCase.explain: The number 10 is 1 ten, which is more than 9 ones. 10 has 1 ten and 9 has 0 tens, so 10 is greater than 9.

reading.title: Treat Jars at the Shelter
reading.text: Hana and Ravi volunteer at the animal shelter. Hana counts 47 dog treats in one jar. Ravi counts 52 treats in another jar. They compare the numbers. First they look at the tens digit. 47 has 4 tens and 52 has 5 tens. Since 5 tens is greater than 4 tens, 52 is greater than 47. Hana writes 52 > 47. Ravi writes 47 < 52 because 47 is less than 52. Then they find a third jar with 52 treats. Hana says the two jars with 52 treats are equal to each other. She writes 52 = 52.
reading.simple: Hana and Ravi volunteer at the animal shelter. Hana has 47 dog treats in a jar. Ravi has 52 treats in a jar. They compare the numbers. They look at the tens digit. 47 has 4 tens and 52 has 5 tens. So 52 is greater than 47. Hana writes 52 > 47. Ravi writes 47 < 52. A third jar has 52 treats. The two jars are equal. Hana writes 52 = 52.

questions.q: How many treats are in Ravi's jar?
Why do Hana and Ravi look at the tens digit first?
questions.a: The tens digits tell which number has more tens, and that decides which number is greater.

questions.q: Which is true: 47 > 52 or 47 < 52?

wdntb.why: 34 = 43 is not true. The other three say the same true thing in different ways.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at these pairs of numbers: 29 and 31, 40 and 38, 55 and 55. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A two-digit number with more tens is greater than a two-digit number with fewer tens.
asn.why: One more ten is worth more than any ones that fit in the ones place.

asn.claim: If two numbers have the same tens digit, they are equal.
asn.why: Numbers like 41 and 47 have the same tens digit, but the ones are different.

wyr.q: Would you rather compare 63 and 58 on a number line or with tens and ones?

compare.a: Nia says 71 is greater than 68 because 7 tens is more than 6 tens.
compare.b: Omar says 68 is greater than 71 because 8 ones is more than 1 one.
compare.prompt: Whose reason works? What should Omar look at first?

debate.claim: You should always compare the tens digits first.
debate.forEvidence: Tens are worth 10 each, so 52 with 5 tens is more than 47 with 4 tens, even though 7 is more than 2.
debate.againstEvidence: If the tens digits are the same, the tens do not decide, and you have to look at the ones.

listening.script: Listen to Yuki at the animal shelter. The blue box has 29 cat toys and the red box has 31 cat toys. I want to compare the numbers, so I look at the tens first. 29 has 2 tens and 31 has 3 tens. Since 3 tens is more than 2 tens, 31 is greater than 29. The red box has more toys. My friend says 29 is greater because 9 is a big digit. But one more ten is worth more than a big ones digit.

tasks.q: Which box has more toys?
tasks.why: 31 has 3 tens and 29 has 2 tens, so 31 is greater and the red box has more.

tasks.q: The friend says 29 is greater because 9 is a big digit. What is the error?
options: The friend looked at the ones digit before the tens digit.
The friend counted the toys twice.
tasks.why: The tens decide first, and 29 has fewer tens than 31.

story.title: Field Day Scores
story.goal: tell which team has the greater score
story.intro: Diego is the scorekeeper at field day, and two teams finish with scores on cards that he must compare.

beats.lead: Diego puts the two score cards side by side.
beats.success: Diego compares the tens first and names the team with the greater score.
beats.redirect: Diego's winner does not look right, so he checks the tens digit before the ones digit.

beats.lead: A team asks Diego to write the comparison with a symbol.
beats.success: Diego writes the symbol so the open side faces the greater score.
beats.redirect: The symbol points the wrong way, so Diego fixes it and reads the sentence aloud.

beats.lead: Two other teams finish with the same score.
beats.success: Diego uses the equal sign and explains that neither team is ahead.
beats.redirect: Diego almost picks a winner, so he checks whether the tens and the ones both match.

story.ending: Every team hears a correct comparison, and Diego can tell why one score is greater, less or equal.

panels.says: My jar has 64 marbles and your jar has 46 marbles.
The two numbers use the same digits, so they must be equal.
Look at the tens digit. 64 has 6 tens and 46 has 4 tens.
So 64 is greater than 46, and I can write 64 > 46.

predict.q: Omar writes the comparison again with 46 first. Before he finishes, predict which symbol is right.
predict.why: 46 has fewer tens than 64, so 46 is less than 64.

transfer.relationship: Compare the tens first, and the symbol shows which number is greater
phrasings: 52 is greater than 47
47 is less than 52

decoys.why: This says 47 is greater, but 47 has fewer tens than 52.
The two numbers are different amounts, so they are not equal.

modeling.title: Comparing weekly pet food cans
modeling.scenario: A fictional animal shelter writes down how many cans of pet food it gives out each week for three weeks.
assumptions: Every can that is given out is counted one time.
Each week has the same number of days.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: Which week gave out the most cans? Which week gave out the fewest?
Write a comparison sentence for two weeks using the symbol > or <.
Which two weeks gave out an equal number of cans? How do you know?
limits: A real shelter has weeks with holidays, so the numbers may change for other reasons.
Comparing numbers does not tell us why one week gave out more cans.

sentence.because: 52 is greater than 47 because 52 has 5 tens and 47 has only 4 tens.
sentence.but: 47 has a bigger ones digit, but 52 is still greater.
sentence.so: 52 has more tens, so 52 is greater than 47.

diagnostic.prompt: Show two cards, 38 and 52. Ask: Which number is greater? How do you know? Then write the comparison with a symbol.
lookFor: Looks at the tens digit first
Writes the symbol so the open side faces the greater number
Gives a reason in a full sentence
diagnostic.language: If the student points to the greater number but cannot say greater than or less than, the barrier is language. Offer the frame: ___ is greater than ___.

extension.task: Find three numbers that are greater than 47 and less than 52. Write a comparison for each number.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know each of your numbers fits, using tens and ones.

en.learning: Your child is learning to compare two numbers up to 100 and to use the signs for greater than, less than and equal to.
en.say: Look at the tens first. The number with more tens is greater.
en.ask: Which is greater, 38 or 52? How do you know?
en.activity: Write two numbers on slips of paper, such as 46 and 64. Take turns choosing the greater one and saying why.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a comparar dos números hasta el 100 y a usar los signos de mayor que, menor que e igual a.
es.say: Miren primero las decenas. El número con más decenas es el mayor.
es.activity: Escriban dos números en papelitos, como 46 y 64. Túrnense para elegir el mayor y decir por qué.

skills.objective: Students understand the equal sign as meaning that both sides are the same amount, decide if equations within 20 are true or false, and find an unknown number in equations with the unknown in any position.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell if an equation is true and find the missing number.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain that both sides are the same using the words equal sign, equation and the same as.
successCriteria: I say that the equal sign means both sides are the same amount.
I find the value of each side and tell if the equation is true or false.
I find the missing number in an equation like 6 + 2 = 4 + ___.
I read an equation like 7 = 3 + 4 and explain why it is true.
skills.bigIdea: The equal sign says that the amount on the left is the same as the amount on the right, so the total can be on either side.

syntax: Both sides are the same amount, so the equation is true.
___ + ___ is the same as ___ + ___.
discourse: Tell a partner how you know an equation is true or false

domains.listening: Students listen to a balance story and say whether the two sides are the same.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner the value of each side and say true or false with a reason.
domains.reading: Students read a short balance story and find each equation and each side.
domains.writing: Students write an equation for a balanced scale and a sentence that says why it is true.

vocab.def: The sign =. It means both sides are the same amount.
vocab.example: In 5 + 3 = 8, the equal sign shows both sides are 8.
vocab.nonExample: The plus sign +, which joins numbers
vocab.sentence: The equal sign tells us both sides are the same.

vocab.def: A number sentence with an equal sign, like 3 + 4 = 7.
vocab.example: 6 + 2 = 8 is an equation.
vocab.nonExample: 6 + 2, which has no equal sign
vocab.sentence: Jabari writes an equation for the balanced scale.

vocab.def: When both sides weigh the same, the scale stays level.
vocab.example: 5 blocks and 3 blocks on one side and 8 blocks on the other side balance.
vocab.nonExample: A scale that tips down on one side
vocab.sentence: The balance stays level when both sides match.
vocab.everyday: To stand or walk without falling over, like balancing on one foot.

vocab.def: Equal in amount. Two things can look different and still match.
vocab.example: 3 + 4 is the same as 5 + 2.
vocab.nonExample: 7 and 4, which are different amounts
vocab.sentence: 7 is the same as 3 + 4.

vocab.def: A number you do not know yet, shown by a box.
vocab.example: In 6 + 2 = 4 + ☐, the box is the unknown.
vocab.nonExample: The number 8, which we already know
vocab.sentence: The unknown number of blocks was 3.

misconceptions.belief: The equal sign means 'the answer comes next'.
misconceptions.why: Most early practice is written as 3 + 4 = 7, so students read the sign as a signal to write an answer.
misconceptions.fix: Use a balance. Put 4 + 3 on one pan and ask what must go on the other pan to make it level.

errorCase.story: Priya solves 4 + 3 = ☐ + 5.
steps: 4 + 3 makes 7.
Priya thinks the equal sign means the answer comes next, so she puts 7 in the box.
She says 4 + 3 = 7 + 5 is true.
errorCase.explain: The equal sign means both sides are the same amount. The left side is 7, so the right side must be 7 too. 2 + 5 = 7, so the box is 2.

misconceptions.belief: 9 = 6 + 3 is wrong because the answer must come after the equal sign.
misconceptions.why: Students have only seen the total written last, so they reject a true equation written in the other direction.
misconceptions.fix: Read it aloud as 'nine is the same as six plus three' and show both sides with counters.

errorCase.story: Samir sees the equation 9 = 6 + 3.
steps: 6 + 3 makes 9.
The 9 is before the equal sign, so Samir says the equation is wrong.
He says 9 = 6 + 3 is false.
errorCase.explain: An equal sign can have the total on either side. 9 and 6 + 3 are the same amount, so 9 = 6 + 3 is true.

misconceptions.belief: 'The same as' means the two sides must look the same.
misconceptions.why: In everyday talk, 'the same' often means 'looks alike', so students reject 3 + 4 = 5 + 2.
misconceptions.fix: Show 3 + 4 and 5 + 2 with counters and ask if the amounts match, even if the groups look different.

misconceptions.belief: To find the missing number, I add every number I can see.
misconceptions.why: Students have practiced putting numbers together, so they join all the numbers in an equation.
misconceptions.fix: Find the value of the side with no unknown first, then ask what makes the other side match.

errorCase.story: Ana has to find the missing number in 5 + 2 = 3 + ☐.
steps: Ana adds every number she sees: 5 + 2 + 3 = 10.
She writes 10 in the box.
errorCase.explain: 5 + 2 is 7, so 3 + ☐ must also be 7. 3 + 4 = 7, so the box is 4.

reading.title: The Science Balance
reading.text: Jabari and Mei use a balance in the science room. They put 5 blocks and 3 blocks on the left side. They put 8 blocks on the right side. The balance stays level. Jabari writes an equation: 5 + 3 = 8. The equal sign shows that both sides are the same. Then Mei puts 7 blocks on the left side and 4 blocks on the right side. The scale tips down on the left. Mei says 7 is not the same as 4. She takes some blocks away from the left side. Now both sides have 4 blocks, and the balance is level again. The unknown number of blocks to take away was 3.
reading.simple: Jabari and Mei use a balance. They put 5 blocks and 3 blocks on the left. They put 8 blocks on the right. The balance is level. Jabari writes an equation: 5 + 3 = 8. The equal sign shows both sides are the same. Then Mei puts 7 blocks on the left and 4 blocks on the right. The scale tips. Mei takes some blocks away from the left. Now both sides have 4. The unknown number was 3.

questions.q: How many blocks are on the right side at the start?
Why does the scale tip down on the left when Mei puts 7 blocks on the left and 4 blocks on the right?
questions.a: The left side has more blocks than the right side, so the sides are not the same.

questions.q: Which equation shows the balanced sides at the start?

wdntb.why: 5 + 3 is 8, not 7, so 7 = 5 + 3 is false. The other three equations are true.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at these: 6 + 2 = 8, 8 = 6 + 2 and 7 + 1 = 8. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: An equation can have the total on the left side of the equal sign.
asn.why: The equal sign only says both sides are the same amount, so either side can hold the total.

asn.claim: If one side of an equation is 9, the other side can be any number.
asn.why: The other side must also be 9 for the equation to be true.

wyr.q: Would you rather show 6 + 2 = 8 on a balance or with two groups of counters?

compare.a: Leo thinks 8 + 4 = 7 + 5 is false because the numbers are different.
compare.prompt: Who is right? How can you tell?

debate.claim: A balance is the best way to show what an equal sign means.
debate.forEvidence: A level balance shows two sides that weigh the same, just like two sides that are the same amount.
debate.againstEvidence: Two groups of counters also show matching sides, and a balance can be hard to set up.

listening.script: Listen to Elena explain her science balance. On the left side I put 6 blocks and 2 blocks. On the right side I put 8 blocks. The balance is level, so I write 6 + 2 = 8. Then my partner puts 9 blocks on the right side and leaves 6 and 2 on the left. The scale tips down on the right. My partner says 9 equals 6 + 2. But 9 is not the same as 8, so it is not true. We take 1 block away from the right side, and the balance is level again.

tasks.q: How many blocks are on the right side when the balance is level?
tasks.why: The right side has 8 blocks, which is the same as 6 + 2.

tasks.q: The partner says 9 = 6 + 2. What is the error?
options: 6 + 2 is 8, not 9, so the sides are not the same.
The equal sign must come at the end.
tasks.why: 6 + 2 is 8, and 8 is not the same amount as 9.

story.title: The Level Scale
story.goal: make both sides of the scale the same and write an equation
story.intro: Ana has a balance scale and a box of blocks, and her teacher asks her to make both sides match and write an equation for each balance.

beats.lead: Ana puts blocks on both sides and watches the scale.
beats.success: The scale is level, so Ana writes an equation with an equal sign.
beats.redirect: The scale tips, so Ana finds the value of each side and sees which side has more.

beats.lead: A friend hides some blocks under a cup and calls them the unknown.
beats.success: Ana finds the unknown number so both sides match.
beats.redirect: Ana's number makes one side bigger, so she tries a different number and checks again.

beats.lead: The class posts equations on the wall, and some have the total written first.
beats.success: Ana reads each one as two sides that are the same, wherever the total is.
beats.redirect: Ana reads one equation as a sentence with the answer next, so she checks both sides again.

story.ending: The scale is level, the wall is full of true equations, and Ana can explain what the equal sign means.

panels.says: I see 5 + 4 = 9 on the board.
Look at 9 = 5 + 4. That must be wrong, because the total is first.
The equal sign means both sides are the same amount. 5 + 4 is 9.
So 9 = 5 + 4 is true, and I can read it from either side.

predict.q: Ana writes 6 + 2 = 4 + ☐. Before she solves it, predict the missing number.
predict.why: 6 + 2 is 8, so the right side must be 8, and 4 + 4 = 8.

transfer.relationship: Both sides of an equation name the same amount
phrasings: A balance with 5 and 3 on one side and 8 on the other side

decoys.why: 5 + 3 is 8, so the two sides are not the same.
Adding 3 to only one side makes the sides different: 8 is not 11.

modeling.title: Balancing the class scale
modeling.scenario: A fictional science class puts marbles in the two pans of a balance. One pan holds 9 marbles and 5 marbles, and the other pan holds 8 marbles and some more.
assumptions: All of the marbles weigh the same.
The scale is level only when both pans hold the same amount.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: How many marbles are in the left pan?
How many more marbles go in the right pan so the pans are equal?
Write an equation with a box for the unknown number in the right pan.
limits: Real marbles can weigh a little different, so a real scale might tip.
The equation tells us how many marbles, not how heavy they are.

sentence.because: 5 + 3 = 8 is true because both sides are the same amount.
sentence.but: 5 + 3 and 6 + 2 look different, but they are equal.
sentence.so: Both sides are 8, so the equal sign is correct.

diagnostic.prompt: Write 7 = 3 + 4 and ask: Is this true or false? How do you know? Then write 6 + 2 = 5 + ☐ and ask for the missing number.
lookFor: Treats the equal sign as 'both sides are the same amount'
Finds the value of each side
Uses an equation to explain the unknown number
diagnostic.language: Let the student show each side with counters or a balance before using words. If the student shows that both sides match, the barrier is the words 'the same as' and 'equal'.

extension.task: Make three equations where both sides equal 10 and each side is an addition, like 4 + 6 = 7 + 3.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know each pair of sides is the same without using the answer-next idea.

en.learning: Your child is learning that the equal sign means both sides are the same amount, so 7 = 3 + 4 is a true equation.
en.say: The equal sign means the same as. Both sides have to match.
en.ask: Is 5 + 2 the same as 3 + 4? How do you know?
en.activity: Put 8 coins on a table. Show 8 as 5 and 3, then as 6 and 2, and say each time that both sides are the same.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo que el signo igual significa que los dos lados tienen la misma cantidad, así que 7 = 3 + 4 es una ecuación verdadera.
es.say: El signo igual quiere decir lo mismo que. Los dos lados deben coincidir.
es.ask: ¿5 + 2 es lo mismo que 3 + 4? ¿Cómo lo sabes?
es.activity: Pongan 8 monedas en la mesa. Muestren el 8 como 5 y 3, y luego como 6 y 2, y digan cada vez que los dos lados son iguales.

skills.objective: Students measure the length of an object with same-size units placed end to end with no gaps or overlaps, say the length as a whole number of units, and compare two lengths that are measured with the same unit.
skills.studentObjective: I can measure how long something is with units and tell which thing is longer.
skills.languageObjective: I will tell how long something is using the words length, unit, end to end and longer.
successCriteria: I start at one end of the object and place units end to end.
I leave no gaps and no overlaps between the units.
I say the length as a number and a unit, like 7 paper clips.
I use the same unit to tell which of two things is longer.
skills.bigIdea: Length is how many same-size units fit along an object from one end to the other, and you can only compare numbers that use the same unit.

syntax: The ___ is ___ paper clips long.
The ___ is longer than the ___ because it takes more units.
discourse: Tell a partner how you measured and what unit you used

domains.listening: Students listen to a ribbon-measuring story and say the length and the unit.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they measured and which object is longer.
domains.reading: Students read a short measuring story and find each object, its length and its unit.
domains.writing: Students write the length of an object with a number and a unit, and a sentence that compares two lengths.

vocab.def: How long something is from one end to the other.
vocab.example: The length of the pencil is 7 paper clips.
vocab.nonExample: How heavy the pencil is
vocab.sentence: The length of each object is a whole number of paper clips.

vocab.def: One copy of a size that you use to measure.
vocab.example: A paper clip can be a unit of length.
vocab.nonExample: A measure with no unit, like just the number 7
vocab.sentence: Ravi and Elena use a paper clip as the unit.
vocab.everyday: One apartment in a building, or one part of a school lesson.

vocab.def: To find how long something is by using units.
vocab.example: Measure the desk with paper clips.
vocab.nonExample: Guess how long the desk is without checking
vocab.sentence: Ravi and Elena measure things in their classroom.

vocab.def: Placed in a line with no gaps, one after another.
vocab.example: Cubes placed end to end along a ribbon
vocab.nonExample: Cubes with a space between each one
vocab.sentence: Ravi puts the clips end to end along the pencil.

vocab.def: Having more length. The other thing is shorter.
vocab.example: A book that is 9 clips long is longer than a pencil that is 7 clips long.
vocab.nonExample: The pencil, which is shorter than the book
vocab.sentence: The book is longer than the pencil.

misconceptions.belief: I can leave a little space between the units and still count them.
misconceptions.why: Students place units where they fit quickly and do not see that a gap is length that nobody counted.
misconceptions.fix: Slide the units together until they touch, and compare the count with the gaps and without the gaps.

errorCase.story: Kofi measures a crayon that is really 5 paper clips long.
steps: Kofi puts 4 paper clips along the crayon and leaves a gap between each clip.
He says the crayon is 4 paper clips long.
errorCase.explain: Units must go end to end with no gaps. The gaps hide part of the length. With no gaps, the crayon is 5 paper clips long.

misconceptions.belief: The thing with the bigger number is always longer.
misconceptions.why: Students compare only the counting numbers and forget that the units can be different sizes.
misconceptions.fix: Measure both objects with the same unit before comparing, and say the unit with each number.

errorCase.story: Mei measures a pencil with small cubes and a book with big blocks.
steps: The pencil is 8 small cubes long.
The book is 5 big blocks long.
8 is more than 5, so Mei says the pencil is longer than the book.
errorCase.explain: The units are different sizes, so the numbers cannot be compared. Measure both objects with the same unit, then compare.

misconceptions.belief: 'Long' and 'longer' mean the same thing.
misconceptions.why: The ending -er changes the meaning to a comparison, but students hear only the word long.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'long' about one thing and 'longer' about two things. Hold up two ribbons and say 'This ribbon is longer than that ribbon.'

reading.title: Measuring with Paper Clips
reading.text: Ravi and Elena measure things in their classroom. They use a paper clip as the unit. Ravi puts the clips end to end along a pencil with no gaps and no overlaps. The pencil is 7 paper clips long. Elena measures a book. She lines up the first clip with the left end of the book. The book is 9 paper clips long. Elena says the book is longer than the pencil, because 9 paper clips is more length than 7 paper clips. Ravi wants to measure the desk with the same unit. He puts down 12 paper clips. The length of the desk is 12 paper clips.
reading.simple: Ravi and Elena measure things. They use a paper clip as the unit. Ravi puts the clips end to end along a pencil. There are no gaps. The pencil is 7 paper clips long. Elena measures a book. It is 9 paper clips long. The book is longer than the pencil. Ravi measures the desk with the same unit. The desk is 12 paper clips long.

questions.q: How many paper clips long is the pencil?
Why is it important that Ravi uses no gaps and no overlaps?
questions.a: Gaps and overlaps change the count, so the length would not be right.

questions.q: How many more paper clips long is the book than the pencil?

wdntb.why: The crayon is measured in cubes. The other three objects are measured in paper clips.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at three objects measured in paper clips: a pencil with 7, a book with 9 and a desk with 12. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: To compare two lengths, measure both objects with the same unit.
asn.why: Only numbers that use the same unit can be compared fairly.

asn.claim: A shorter unit makes the number of units smaller.
asn.why: A shorter unit fits more times along the object, so the number gets bigger.

wyr.q: Would you rather measure your desk with paper clips or with cubes?

compare.a: Diego lays 6 cubes end to end with no gaps along a ribbon.
compare.b: Lin lays 6 cubes along the same ribbon with a gap between each cube.
compare.prompt: Whose measure is correct? Tell what Lin should change.

debate.claim: Smaller units are better for measuring than bigger units.
debate.forEvidence: A small cube can show that a ribbon is a little more than 6 cubes long, so the measure is closer.
debate.againstEvidence: Smaller units mean more units to count, so it takes longer and it is easier to lose count.

listening.script: Listen to Nia tell about measuring a ribbon. I use cubes as my unit. I put the cubes end to end along the ribbon. I start at the left end and leave no gaps. I count 10 cubes, so the ribbon is 10 cubes long. My friend measures a string with paper clips and gets 8 paper clips. He says the ribbon is longer because 10 is more than 8. But we used different units, so we cannot compare the numbers. When we measure the string with cubes, it is 14 cubes long. So the string is longer.

tasks.q: How many cubes long is the ribbon?
tasks.why: Nia counts 10 cubes end to end along the ribbon.

tasks.q: The friend says the ribbon is longer because 10 is more than 8. What is the error?
options: The two measures use different units, so the numbers cannot be compared.
The friend should have counted the ribbon twice.
tasks.why: 10 cubes and 8 paper clips use different units, so they must be measured with the same unit before comparing.

story.title: The Longest Ribbon
story.goal: find the longest ribbon for the puppet stage curtain
story.intro: Priya has three ribbons for the class puppet show, and she needs the longest one for the curtain and a bin of cubes to measure with.

beats.lead: Priya lines up the first cube with the end of the first ribbon.
beats.success: Priya places cubes end to end with no gaps and counts the length.
beats.redirect: A gap shows between two cubes, so Priya pushes them together and counts again.
