beats.lead: A friend measures a second ribbon with paper clips instead of cubes.
beats.success: Priya asks for the same unit, and now both lengths can be compared.
beats.redirect: The numbers use different units, so Priya measures both ribbons with cubes.

beats.lead: Priya must pick the longest ribbon for the curtain.
beats.success: She compares the lengths and picks the ribbon that takes the most cubes.
beats.redirect: Priya checks that every ribbon was measured with cubes before she chooses.

story.ending: The longest ribbon hangs on the puppet stage, and Priya can tell how she measured and compared.

panels.says: My shoe is 9 small blocks long.
My shoe is 6 big blocks long, so yours is longer because 9 is more.
Wait. My blocks are small and your blocks are big.
Let us both measure with the same small blocks, then compare.

predict.q: Priya and Diego measure the same table with different units. Before they measure, predict who gets the bigger number.
options: The person with the smaller unit
The person with the bigger unit
They always get the same number
predict.why: A smaller unit fits more times along the table, so the number is bigger.

transfer.relationship: Length is the number of same-size units laid end to end with no gaps or overlaps
phrasings: The pencil is 7 paper clips long
7 paper clips laid end to end match the pencil
From one end to the other, the pencil is 7 clips
Pencil length: 7 clips (the unit is a paper clip)

decoys.why: Without a unit, we do not know what the 7 counts.

decoys.text: The pencil is 7 clips long, with a gap between each clip
decoys.why: Gaps change the count, so the length would not be right.

modeling.title: Choosing a ribbon for the stage
modeling.scenario: A fictional class measures three ribbons with cubes to decide which one to use for a puppet stage. The ribbons are red, blue and green.
assumptions: All of the cubes are the same size.
Every ribbon is measured end to end with no gaps or overlaps.
The ribbons stay straight while they are measured.
prompts: Which ribbon is the longest? Which ribbon is the shortest?
How many more cubes long is the green ribbon than the red ribbon?
The stage curtain needs a ribbon at least 12 cubes long. Which ribbons are long enough?
limits: Real ribbons stretch a little, so the count could change.
Cubes are not an exact standard unit like a centimeter.

sentence.base: The pencil is 7 paper clips long.
sentence.because: The pencil is 7 paper clips long because 7 paper clips fit end to end along it.
sentence.but: The pencil is shorter than the book, but both were measured with paper clips.
sentence.so: The pencil takes 7 clips and the book takes 9 clips, so the book is longer.

diagnostic.prompt: Give the student a pencil and 10 cubes. Ask: How long is the pencil? Show me how you measured.
lookFor: Starts at one end of the object
Places the units end to end with no gaps or overlaps
States the length with a number and a unit
diagnostic.language: If the student lays the cubes correctly but cannot name the unit, the barrier is language. Ask the student to point to the unit and say 'cubes'.

extension.task: Measure your desk with two different units. Before you measure, predict which unit gives the bigger number.
extension.reasoning: Explain why the two numbers are different even though the desk is the same length.

en.learning: Your child is learning to measure length by lining up same-size units, like paper clips or blocks, with no gaps.
en.say: Start at one end and put the units next to each other with no space between them.
en.ask: How long is it? What unit did you use?
en.activity: Measure a shoe, a spoon and a book with the same small object, such as a coin. Say which is longest and how you know.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a medir la longitud alineando unidades del mismo tamaño, como clips o bloques, sin dejar espacios.
es.say: Empiecen en un extremo y pongan las unidades una al lado de otra, sin espacio entre ellas.
es.activity: Midan un zapato, una cuchara y un libro con el mismo objeto pequeño, como una moneda. Digan cuál es el más largo y cómo lo saben.

skills.objective: Students read and write time to the hour and half hour on an analog clock, using the short hour hand to name the hour and the long minute hand to tell o'clock or half past.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell time to the hour and half hour.
skills.languageObjective: I will tell the time using the words hour hand, minute hand, o'clock and half past.
successCriteria: I use the short hand to name the hour.
I use the long hand to tell if it is o'clock or half past.
I say and write times such as 8 o'clock and half past 9.
I draw the hands on a clock to show a time.
skills.bigIdea: The short hand tells the hour, and the long hand tells whether it is o'clock or half past the hour.

syntax: The short hand points to ___ and the long hand points to ___.
It is half past ___.
discourse: Tell a partner how you know the hour and the half hour

domains.listening: Students listen to a morning routine and match each event to a clock time.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner a time and describe where each hand points.
domains.reading: Students read a short bus story and find each time and each clue about the hands.
domains.writing: Students write a time in words and in numbers and draw the hands.

vocab.def: A pointer on a clock that shows the time.
vocab.example: A clock has a short hand and a long hand.
vocab.nonExample: The numbers around the edge of the clock
vocab.sentence: The short hand points to 8.
vocab.everyday: The body part at the end of your arm.

vocab.def: The short hand. It tells the hour.
vocab.example: At 4 o'clock the hour hand points to 4.
vocab.nonExample: The long hand, which tells minutes
vocab.sentence: The hour hand has not reached 10, so the hour is still 9.

vocab.def: The long hand. It tells the minutes.
vocab.example: At half past the hour the minute hand points to 6.
vocab.nonExample: The short hand, which tells the hour
vocab.sentence: The minute hand points to 12 at 8 o'clock.

vocab.def: How we say the time when the minute hand points to 12.
vocab.example: 7 o'clock
vocab.nonExample: Half past 7, when the long hand points to 6
vocab.sentence: The bus leaves at 8 o'clock.

vocab.def: Thirty minutes after the hour. The minute hand points to 6.
vocab.example: Half past 7 is 7:30.
vocab.nonExample: 7 o'clock, when the minute hand points to 12
vocab.sentence: At half past 9 the class goes to the library.

misconceptions.belief: The long hand tells the hour.
misconceptions.why: The long hand is the one that stands out, so students read the number it points to as the hour.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'short hand, hour' every time. Put a short paper hand and a long paper hand on a clock and move only the long one.

errorCase.story: Zara looks at a clock where the short hand points to 4 and the long hand points to 12.
steps: The short hand points to 4 and the long hand points to 12.
Zara thinks the long hand tells the hour, so she reads the 12.
She says the time is 12 o'clock.
errorCase.explain: The short hand tells the hour. It points to 4, and the long hand on 12 means o'clock, so the time is 4 o'clock.

misconceptions.belief: At half past 7, the hour is 8 because the hour hand is near the 8.
misconceptions.why: At half past, the hour hand sits halfway between two numbers, and students name the number it is closer to or heading toward.
misconceptions.fix: Move the hour hand slowly from 7 to 8 and show that the hour is 7 until the hand reaches the 8.

errorCase.story: Omar looks at a clock where the hour hand is halfway between 7 and 8 and the minute hand points to 6.
steps: The minute hand points to 6, so it is half past.
The hour hand is past the 7 but has not reached the 8.
Omar says the time is half past 8.
errorCase.explain: The hour hand has not reached 8, so the hour is still 7. The time is half past 7, or 7:30.

misconceptions.belief: 'Half past 7' means the time is before 7.
misconceptions.why: The word half sounds like a part of 7, and past is easy to mix up with 'to' or 'before'.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'half past 7 means 7 o'clock has already gone by, and half an hour more.' Show the minute hand going halfway around.

misconceptions.belief: When the long hand points to 6, the time is 6 o'clock.
misconceptions.why: Students read the number the long hand points to as the answer, without checking which hand it is.
misconceptions.fix: Always find the short hand first and say the hour. Then look at the long hand for o'clock or half past.

reading.title: Bus Time at School
reading.text: Nia and Leo ride the school bus. Nia looks at a clock. The short hand points to 8 and the long hand points to 12. It is 8 o'clock, and the bus leaves. Later, Leo looks at the clock in the classroom. The long hand points to 6, and the short hand is between 9 and 10. Leo says the time is half past 9. That is 30 minutes after 9 o'clock. At half past 9 the class goes to the library. Nia says the hour hand has not reached 10, so the hour is still 9. They draw both clocks and label each hand.
reading.simple: Nia and Leo ride the school bus. Nia looks at a clock. The short hand points to 8. The long hand points to 12. It is 8 o'clock. Later, Leo looks at the clock in the classroom. The long hand points to 6. The short hand is between 9 and 10. It is half past 9. That is 30 minutes after 9. Nia says the hour hand has not reached 10.

questions.q: What time does the bus leave?
Why is the hour still 9 when the short hand is between 9 and 10?
questions.a: The hour hand has not reached 10 yet, so the hour is still 9.

questions.q: How many minutes after 9 o'clock is half past 9?

wdntb.why: At half past 3 the minute hand points to 6. At the other three times it points to 12.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at two clocks. On one, the long hand points to 12. On the other, the long hand points to 6. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: When the minute hand points to 12, the time is an o'clock time.
asn.why: The minute hand on 12 means no minutes have passed after the hour.

asn.claim: At half past the hour, the hour hand points exactly at a number.
asn.why: At half past, the hour hand is halfway between two numbers.

wyr.q: Would you rather read time on a clock with hands or on a clock with only numbers?

compare.a: Ana says the time is half past 5 because the short hand is between 5 and 6.
compare.b: Ben says the time is half past 6 because the short hand is near the 6.
compare.prompt: Who is right? What does the hour hand tell you?

debate.claim: It is easier to read time on a clock with hands than on a screen with numbers.
debate.forEvidence: A clock with hands shows how far the time has moved, and half past looks like the minute hand halfway around.
debate.againstEvidence: A screen with numbers shows the time right away, so you do not have to read two hands.

listening.script: Listen to Hana tell about her morning. I wake up at 7 o'clock. The short hand points to 7 and the long hand points to 12. I eat breakfast until half past 7. At half past 7 the long hand points to 6, and the short hand is halfway between 7 and 8. My brother says it is 8 o'clock because the short hand is near the 8. But the short hand has not reached the 8 yet. So the hour is still 7, and it is half past 7.

tasks.q: What time is it when the long hand points to 6 and the short hand is halfway between 7 and 8?
tasks.why: The long hand on 6 means half past, and the hour hand has not reached 8, so the hour is 7.

tasks.q: Hana's brother says it is 8 o'clock. What is the error?
options: The short hand has not reached 8, so the hour is still 7.
The long hand always tells the hour.
tasks.why: The hour hand is between 7 and 8 and has not reached 8, and the long hand is on 6.

story.title: Ready for the Bus
story.goal: be at the bus stop at the right time
story.intro: Jabari wears a watch with two hands, and the bus comes at an o'clock time while the class trip starts at a half past time.

beats.lead: Jabari looks at his watch to see if it is time for the bus.
beats.success: Jabari reads the short hand first, says the hour, and then checks the long hand.
beats.redirect: Jabari read the long hand as the hour, so he starts again with the short hand.

beats.lead: The teacher says the trip starts at half past the hour.
beats.success: Jabari finds the long hand on 6 and the hour hand between two numbers.
beats.redirect: Jabari names the wrong hour, so he checks which number the hour hand has already passed.

beats.lead: The class draws the hands on paper clocks to show their times.
beats.success: Jabari draws a short hand and a long hand, and each one is in the right place.
beats.redirect: The two hands look the same length, so Jabari makes the hour hand shorter.

story.ending: The bus leaves on time, and Jabari can tell the hour and the half hour from both hands.

panels.says: My watch has the long hand on 12 and the short hand on 3.
That means it is 3 o'clock.
Now the long hand is on 6. Is it 6 o'clock?
No. The long hand on 6 means half past, and the short hand tells the hour.

predict.q: Jabari's watch shows the long hand on 6 and the short hand between 3 and 4. Before Zara answers, predict the time.
predict.why: The hour hand has not reached 4, so the hour is 3, and the long hand on 6 means half past.

transfer.relationship: The short hand names the hour, and the long hand shows o'clock or half past
phrasings: It is 7 o'clock
The time is 7:00
The short hand points to 7 and the long hand points to 12
The hour is 7 and no minutes have gone by

decoys.why: This reads the long hand as the hour, but the short hand points to 7.
7:30 needs the long hand on 6, but here it points to 12.

modeling.title: Planning the class day
modeling.scenario: A fictional class has a schedule with times on the hour and on the half hour. The teacher wants students to read each time on a clock.
assumptions: Every activity starts exactly on time.
The clock in the room is correct.
The times are invented for this exercise.
prompts: Put the three activities in order from first to last.
Draw a clock for the library time. Where does each hand point?
What time is it 1 hour after math starts? Use a clock to check.
limits: A real school schedule can change because of a fire drill or a late bus.
In this activity the clock only shows times on the hour and half hour.

sentence.because: It is half past 7 because the hour hand is past 7 and the minute hand is on 6.
sentence.but: The hour hand is near 8, but the hour is still 7.
sentence.so: The minute hand points to 6, so the time is half past the hour.

diagnostic.prompt: Show a clock set to 4 o'clock and a clock set to half past 4. Ask: What time does each clock show? How do you know?
lookFor: Names the hour from the short hand
Uses the long hand to say o'clock or half past
Does not name the next hour at half past
diagnostic.language: If the student moves the hands to the right places but cannot say the time, the barrier is language. Offer the frame: The short hand points to ___ and the long hand points to ___.

extension.task: Draw a clock for the time your class eats lunch. Then draw a clock for a half hour later.
extension.reasoning: Explain what happens to the minute hand and to the hour hand when a half hour goes by.

en.learning: Your child is learning to tell time to the hour and half hour on a clock with hands.
en.say: Find the short hand first. It tells the hour. Then look at the long hand.
en.ask: What time is it? Where is the short hand and where is the long hand?
en.activity: Use a clock at home. Each time the hour or half hour comes, ask your child to say the time and where each hand points.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a decir la hora en punto y la media hora en un reloj con manecillas.
es.say: Busquen primero la manecilla corta. Dice la hora. Luego miren la manecilla larga.
es.ask: ¿Qué hora es? ¿Dónde está la manecilla corta y dónde está la larga?
es.activity: Usen un reloj de la casa. Cada vez que llegue una hora en punto o una media hora, pidan a su hijo o hija que diga la hora y dónde señala cada manecilla.

skills.objective: Students identify and describe triangles, squares, rectangles and circles by their defining parts, such as the number of sides and corners, and they build new shapes by putting shapes together.
skills.studentObjective: I can name shapes and tell about their sides and corners.
skills.languageObjective: I will describe shapes using the words side, corner, triangle, square and circle in the sentence 'It has ___ sides and ___ corners.'
successCriteria: I count the sides and the corners of a shape.
I name a shape by its sides and corners, not by its size or how it is turned.
I tell why a shape is not a triangle or not a square.
I put two shapes together and tell about the new shape.
skills.bigIdea: A shape keeps its name when it gets bigger, smaller or turned, because its sides and corners stay the same.

syntax: It has ___ sides and ___ corners.
It is a ___ because it has ___.
discourse: Describe a shape so that a partner can name it

domains.listening: Students listen to a shape description and decide which shape the speaker built.
domains.speaking: Students describe a hidden shape by its sides and corners so a partner can guess it.
domains.reading: Students read a short shape-walk story and find each shape and its parts.
domains.writing: Students write a sentence that names a shape and tells its number of sides and corners.

vocab.def: A straight line that is part of the edge of a shape.
vocab.example: A triangle has 3 sides.
vocab.nonExample: The curved edge of a circle
vocab.sentence: Hana counts each side of the triangle.
vocab.everyday: The left or right part of something, like the side of a bed.

vocab.def: The point where two sides of a shape meet.
vocab.example: A square has 4 corners.
vocab.nonExample: The middle of a side
vocab.sentence: Hana turns the square so one corner points up.
vocab.everyday: The place where two walls or two streets meet.

vocab.def: A shape with 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
vocab.example: A yellow sign with 3 sides and 3 corners
vocab.nonExample: A shape with 4 sides
vocab.sentence: The yellow sign is a triangle.

vocab.def: A shape with 4 sides the same length and 4 corners.
vocab.example: A window with 4 equal sides
vocab.nonExample: A door, which has two sides longer than the other two
vocab.sentence: A square can turn and still be a square.
vocab.everyday: An open place in a town where people meet.

vocab.def: A round shape with no sides and no corners.
vocab.example: A plate
vocab.nonExample: A triangle, which has straight sides
vocab.sentence: A circle has 0 sides and 0 corners.

misconceptions.belief: A square turned so a corner points up is not a square. It is a diamond.
misconceptions.why: Students often see shapes in only one position, so a turned shape looks like a different shape.
misconceptions.fix: Turn a paper square in every direction and count its sides and corners each time. Say 'Still 4 and 4.'

errorCase.story: Mei turns a paper square so a corner points up.
steps: The shape still has 4 sides the same length and 4 corners.
Mei turns it and says it is a new shape called a diamond.
She says it is not a square any more.
errorCase.explain: Turning a shape does not change its sides or corners. It still has 4 equal sides and 4 corners, so it is still a square.

misconceptions.belief: Corners and sides are two different groups, so I add them.
misconceptions.why: Students count the parts they see without noticing that every corner sits between two sides.
misconceptions.fix: Trace each side with a finger and put a dot at each corner. Show that a triangle has 3 dots and 3 lines, not 6 of one thing.

errorCase.story: Kofi counts the parts of a triangle.
steps: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
Kofi counts the sides and then counts the corners as if they were more sides.
He says a triangle has 6 sides.
errorCase.explain: A corner is a point where two sides meet. It is not another side. The triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.

misconceptions.belief: A side of a shape is the flat top or front, like the side of a box.
misconceptions.why: In everyday talk 'side' means the left or right part of a thing, so students do not hear it as a straight edge.
misconceptions.fix: Trace each side of a flat shape with a finger and say 'one side, two sides, three sides.'

reading.title: The Shape Walk
reading.text: Zara and Omar go on a shape walk in the neighborhood. Zara sees a yellow sign with 3 sides and 3 corners. It is a triangle. Omar finds a window with 4 sides the same length and 4 corners. It is a square. Zara turns her paper square so one corner points up. She says it is still a square, because turning does not change the sides or the corners. Then Omar finds a plate. It is a circle. A circle has 0 sides and 0 corners. At home they put a triangle on top of a square to make a house shape. The new shape has 5 sides.
reading.simple: Zara and Omar go on a shape walk. Zara sees a yellow sign with 3 sides and 3 corners. It is a triangle. Omar finds a window with 4 sides the same length and 4 corners. It is a square. Zara turns a paper square. It is still a square. Omar finds a plate. It is a circle. A circle has 0 sides and 0 corners. They put a triangle on a square to make a house. The house has 5 sides.

questions.q: How many sides does the triangle on the yellow sign have?
Why is the turned paper still a square?
questions.a: Turning does not change the number of sides, how long they are, or the corners.

questions.q: How many sides does the house shape made from a triangle and a square have?

wdntb.why: The circle has no corners and no straight sides. The other three shapes have straight sides and corners.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at a triangle, a square and a circle. Count the sides and the corners of each one. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A shape with 4 sides is a square.
asn.why: A square has 4 sides, but a shape with 4 sides can be a rectangle that is not a square.

asn.claim: A square turned on a corner is not a square.
asn.why: Turning does not change the sides or corners, so it is still a square.

wyr.q: Would you rather build a picture with triangles or with squares?

compare.a: Kofi says a shape is a triangle because it has 3 sides.
compare.b: Aisha says a shape is a triangle because it is pointy at the top.

debate.claim: Counting sides and corners is the best way to name a shape.
debate.forEvidence: A triangle always has 3 sides and 3 corners, no matter how big it is or how it is turned.
debate.againstEvidence: A circle has no sides or corners, so counting does not help. You have to look at the round edge.

listening.script: Listen to Aisha tell about her shape picture. I made a house with a square and a triangle. The square has 4 sides the same length and 4 corners. The triangle sits on top and has 3 sides and 3 corners. When I put them together, they share one side. The whole house has 5 sides. My brother says the roof has 4 corners. I count again: 1, 2, 3. A triangle has 3 corners, not 4.

tasks.q: How many sides does the whole house shape have?
tasks.why: The square and the triangle share one side, so the house has 5 sides.

tasks.q: Aisha's brother says the triangle roof has 4 corners. What is the error?
options: A triangle has 3 corners, so he counted one too many.
tasks.why: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.

story.title: Shape Sort at the Park
story.goal: sort the shape cards on the picnic table
story.intro: Leo has a stack of shape cards and three trays at the picnic table, one for triangles, one for squares and one for circles.

beats.lead: Leo picks up a card and counts its sides and its corners.
beats.success: Leo counts the same number of sides and corners and names the shape.
beats.redirect: Leo counted a corner as a side, so he traces each side with a finger and counts again.

beats.lead: A friend turns a square card so a corner points up.
beats.success: Leo counts 4 sides and 4 corners and puts the card in the square tray.
beats.redirect: Leo wants a new tray for the turned card, so he counts its parts and sees nothing changed.

beats.lead: A friend gives Leo a card with a curved edge and no corners.
beats.success: Leo puts the card in the circle tray and says why.
beats.redirect: Leo tries the triangle tray, so he checks for straight sides and finds there are none.

story.ending: Every card is in the right tray, and Leo can tell how many sides and corners each shape has.

panels.says: I made a square with 4 sides.
Now I turn it so a corner points up. It is a diamond!
Count the sides and the corners. Are they the same as before?
Yes, 4 sides and 4 corners. It is still a square, just turned.

predict.q: Mei turns a triangle so a corner points down. Before she counts, predict how many sides it has now.
predict.why: Turning does not change the number of sides, so a triangle still has 3 sides.

transfer.relationship: A shape is named by its sides and corners, not by its size or how it is turned
phrasings: It has 3 sides and 3 corners
It is a triangle
3 straight sides meet at 3 corners
A closed shape with three straight edges and three points

decoys.text: It has 4 corners, so it is a triangle
decoys.why: A triangle has 3 corners, so a shape with 4 corners is not a triangle.

decoys.text: It is a triangle because it is small and pointy
decoys.why: Size and pointiness do not name a triangle. Its 3 sides and 3 corners do.

modeling.title: A tile poster
modeling.scenario: A fictional art class makes a poster out of paper tiles. The poster uses some triangle tiles and some square tiles.
assumptions: Every triangle tile has 3 sides.
Every square tile has 4 sides and 4 corners.
The tiles do not overlap on the poster.
prompts: How many tiles are on the poster?
How many sides do all the triangle tiles have together?
How many corners do all the square tiles have together?
limits: Real paper tiles may be cut a little unevenly, so the sides might not be exactly the same.
Counting sides and corners does not tell us how big each tile is.

sentence.base: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
sentence.because: The shape is a triangle because it has 3 straight sides and 3 corners.
sentence.but: The triangle was turned, but it still has 3 sides.
sentence.so: A square has 4 sides the same length, so it is not a triangle.

diagnostic.prompt: Show a paper triangle, a paper square and a paper circle. Turn each one. Ask the student to name each shape and tell how many sides and corners it has.
lookFor: Counts sides and corners correctly
Names each shape by its parts, even when it is turned
Says that a circle has no sides and no corners
diagnostic.language: If the student sorts the shapes correctly but cannot name them, the barrier is language. Let the student match each shape to a name card before saying the name.

extension.task: Put two triangles together to make a new shape. Draw it and count its sides and its corners.
extension.reasoning: Explain how you know your new shape has the number of sides you counted.

en.learning: Your child is learning to name shapes by their sides and corners, like a triangle with 3 sides and 3 corners.
en.say: A shape keeps its name when you turn it. Count the sides and the corners to be sure.
en.ask: What shape do you see? How many sides and corners does it have?
en.activity: Go on a shape walk at home or outside. Find a triangle, a square and a circle, and count the sides of each.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a nombrar figuras por sus lados y esquinas, como un triángulo con 3 lados y 3 esquinas.
es.say: Una figura conserva su nombre cuando la giran. Cuenten los lados y las esquinas para estar seguros.
es.ask: ¿Qué figura ves? ¿Cuántos lados y esquinas tiene?
es.activity: Salgan a buscar figuras en casa o afuera. Encuentren un triángulo, un cuadrado y un círculo, y cuenten los lados de cada uno.

skills.objective: Students solve addition and subtraction story problems within 20 for stories that join, separate, put parts together and compare, including stories where the start or a part is unknown, by modeling what is happening before choosing an operation.
skills.studentObjective: I can tell what is happening in a story and write a number sentence to solve it.
skills.languageObjective: I will retell a number story and explain my number sentence using the words join, left, fewer and more than.
successCriteria: I retell what is happening in the story in my own words.
I tell if the group gets bigger, gets smaller, or if two groups are compared.
I write a number sentence that matches the story and find the unknown number.
I check that my answer makes sense for the story.
skills.bigIdea: The operation comes from what is happening in the story, not from the numbers you see, and a story can hide the unknown at the start, in the middle or at the end.

syntax: First there were ___. Then ___ came. Now there are ___.
The group got ___ because ___.
discourse: Retell the story to a partner before solving it

domains.listening: Students listen to a pond story and decide whether the group gets bigger or smaller.
domains.speaking: Students retell a number story with First, Then and Now and explain which number is unknown.
domains.reading: Students read a short bake sale story and match each part of it to a number sentence.
domains.writing: Students write a number story and the number sentence that goes with it.

vocab.def: To put two groups together to make one bigger group.
vocab.example: 6 muffins and 7 more muffins join to make 13 muffins.
vocab.nonExample: Some muffins are sold and taken away
vocab.sentence: Yuki will join 7 more muffins to the group.
vocab.everyday: To become a member of a group, like joining a club.

vocab.def: What stays after some are taken away.
vocab.example: 13 muffins, 4 are sold, so 9 muffins are left.
vocab.nonExample: The muffins that were sold
vocab.sentence: There are 9 muffins left on the table.
vocab.everyday: The side that is the opposite of right.

vocab.def: Not as many. A smaller number of things.
vocab.example: 5 cookies is fewer than 8 cookies.
vocab.nonExample: 8 cookies when the other group has 5
vocab.sentence: Samir has 3 fewer cookies than Yuki.

vocab.def: A bigger number of things than another group.
vocab.example: 8 cookies is more than 5 cookies.
vocab.nonExample: 5 cookies when the other group has 8
vocab.sentence: Yuki has 8 cookies, which is more than the 5 cookies Samir has.

vocab.def: A math sentence with numbers and signs, like 8 − 3 = 5.
vocab.nonExample: A sentence with only words and no numbers
vocab.sentence: Samir writes a number sentence for each story.

misconceptions.belief: A story with two numbers is always an addition story.
misconceptions.why: Early practice mostly joins groups, so students join whatever numbers they see instead of picturing the story.
misconceptions.fix: Act out the story with counters first. Ask 'Did the group get bigger or smaller?' before writing a sign.

errorCase.story: A story says: Ana has 12 apples and gives 5 apples to a friend. How many apples does Ana have left?
steps: Ana starts with 12 apples and gives 5 away.
A student sees the numbers 12 and 5 and adds them: 12 + 5 = 17.
The student says Ana has 17 apples left.
errorCase.explain: Giving apples away makes the group smaller, so the answer must be less than 12. 12 − 5 = 7, so Ana has 7 apples left.

misconceptions.belief: When the story does not say how many there were at the start, I add the two numbers I know.
misconceptions.why: Students do not picture the whole story, so they join the numbers they can see.
misconceptions.fix: Draw a box for the unknown start, then show the 5 that came, then the 12 at the end. Ask which number is the biggest.

errorCase.story: Some birds were in a tree. 5 more birds came. Now there are 12 birds. How many birds were in the tree at first?
steps: The story ends with 12 birds, and 5 birds joined.
Leo adds the numbers he sees: 5 + 12 = 17.
He says there were 17 birds at first.
errorCase.explain: The birds at first plus 5 more make 12, so the first group is smaller than 12. 12 − 5 = 7, so there were 7 birds at first.

misconceptions.belief: When a story asks how many more one group has, the answer is the size of the bigger group.
misconceptions.why: Students name the group that has more and forget that the question asks for the difference between the groups.
misconceptions.fix: Line up the two groups in two rows and match them one to one. The extra ones are the answer.

errorCase.story: Nia has 9 stickers and Omar has 6 stickers. How many more stickers does Nia have?
steps: Nia has 9 stickers and Omar has 6 stickers.
The student says the answer is 9 because Nia has the most stickers.
The student says Nia has 9 more stickers.
errorCase.explain: The question asks how much bigger 9 is than 6. Match 6 stickers with 6 of Nia's, and 3 are left over. 9 − 6 = 3, so Nia has 3 more.

misconceptions.belief: 'Left' in a story means the left side.
misconceptions.why: The word left has two meanings, and students know the direction meaning well.
misconceptions.fix: Read the whole sentence: '9 muffins are left on the table.' Ask 'Left after what happened?' and act it out.

reading.title: The Bake Sale Table
reading.text: Samir and Yuki help at the school bake sale. Samir puts 6 muffins on the table. Then Yuki joins 7 more muffins to the group. Now there are 13 muffins. A customer buys 4 muffins. Now 9 muffins are left. Later Yuki counts 8 cookies and Samir counts 5 cookies. Yuki has 3 more cookies than Samir, and Samir has 3 fewer cookies than Yuki. Samir writes a number sentence for each story: 6 + 7 = 13, 13 − 4 = 9 and 8 − 5 = 3. Each number sentence matches what is happening in its story.
reading.simple: Samir and Yuki help at the bake sale. Samir puts 6 muffins on the table. Yuki joins 7 more muffins. Now there are 13 muffins. A customer buys 4 muffins. Now 9 muffins are left. Yuki has 8 cookies and Samir has 5 cookies. Yuki has 3 more than Samir. Samir writes a number sentence for each story: 6 + 7 = 13, 13 − 4 = 9 and 8 − 5 = 3.

questions.q: How many muffins are on the table after Yuki joins 7 more?
Why does Samir subtract in the story about the customer?
questions.a: The customer takes muffins away, so the group gets smaller.

questions.q: How many more cookies does Yuki have than Samir?

wdntb.why: The first three use the same three numbers: 6, 7 and 13. The fourth uses a different total, 19.

noticeWonder.prompt: Read this story: 9 birds are in a tree. 4 birds fly away. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: In a story where some are taken away, the number left is smaller than the number you start with.
asn.why: Taking some away leaves fewer than there were at the start.

asn.claim: A story with two numbers always uses addition.
asn.why: Stories can join, take away or compare, so the story decides the operation.

wyr.q: Would you rather act out a story with counters or draw it as a picture?

compare.a: Hana draws 8 circles, crosses out 3 and counts 5 left.
compare.prompt: Do both ways solve the story? How are they alike?

debate.claim: Drawing a picture is the best way to solve a story.
debate.forEvidence: A picture shows what is happening, so you can see if the group gets bigger or smaller.
debate.againstEvidence: Writing a number sentence is faster and works for bigger numbers, when drawing would take too long.

listening.script: Listen to Ravi's story. There are 8 ducks on a pond. 5 more ducks swim over to the pond. Now there are 13 ducks. Then 6 ducks swim away. I want to know how many ducks are left. I think about what is happening: the group gets smaller. So I subtract. 13 minus 6 is 7. My friend says to add 13 and 6 because there are two numbers. But the ducks swam away, so adding would make a bigger group.

tasks.q: How many ducks are on the pond after 6 swim away?
tasks.why: There are 13 ducks and 6 swim away, so 13 − 6 = 7 ducks are left.

tasks.q: Ravi's friend wants to add 13 and 6. What is the error?
options: The ducks swam away, so the group gets smaller and we subtract.
tasks.why: When ducks swim away, the group gets smaller, so the story needs subtraction.

story.title: The Lemonade Stand
story.goal: keep track of the paper cups as friends add and take cups
story.intro: Hana runs a small lemonade stand with a stack of paper cups, and she writes a number sentence each time the stack changes.

beats.lead: A neighbor brings some more cups to the stand.
beats.success: Hana sees the stack get bigger and writes an addition sentence that matches.
beats.redirect: Hana's answer is smaller than the stack she started with, so she checks that she joined the cups.

beats.lead: Customers use some of the cups on a hot afternoon.
beats.success: Hana sees the stack get smaller and subtracts to find how many are left.
beats.redirect: Hana's answer is bigger than the stack she started with, so she rethinks what happened.

beats.lead: Hana's cousin asks how many more cups the stand has than the neighbor's stand.
beats.success: Hana lines up both stacks and finds how many are extra.
beats.redirect: Hana named the size of the bigger stack, so she matches the two stacks again and counts the extra cups.

story.ending: The stand sells out, and Hana can tell what happened to the cups in every part of the day.

panels.says: I had some stickers. Then I got 4 more, and now I have 11.
The start is unknown. I will add 4 and 11.
Think about what happened. The 4 stickers joined the group I had.
So the stickers you had plus 4 make 11. I subtract 4 from 11 to get 7.

predict.q: A box has some crayons. 3 more crayons are put in, and now there are 10. Before anyone solves it, predict how many crayons were in the box at first.
predict.why: The first group plus 3 makes 10, so the first group is smaller than 10. 10 − 3 = 7.

transfer.relationship: Two parts and a total: if you know any two of them, you can find the third
phrasings: 6 and 7 are the parts and 13 is the total

decoys.why: The total is the biggest number, so it cannot be the answer to an addition of 6 and 13.
Taking 6 away from 13 leaves less than 13, not 19.

modeling.title: Tracking muffins at the bake sale
modeling.scenario: A fictional class sells muffins at a bake sale. They start with some muffins, and then parents bring more.
assumptions: Every muffin that is sold is counted once.
No muffin is dropped or eaten.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: How many muffins are there after the parents bring 4 more?
How many muffins are left after 9 are sold?
Write a number sentence for each change.
limits: A real bake sale has sizes and prices that these numbers do not show.
We did not count the muffins that are baked later in the day.

sentence.because: 13 − 4 = 9 matches the story because 4 muffins were taken away from 13 muffins.
sentence.but: The story has two numbers, but we subtract and do not add.
sentence.so: Some muffins were sold, so there are fewer left.

diagnostic.prompt: Tell the story: 9 birds are in a tree, and some more join. Now there are 14 birds. Ask: How many birds joined? Draw it and write a number sentence.
lookFor: Retells what happened before choosing an operation
Writes a number sentence that matches the story, such as 9 + ☐ = 14 or 14 − 9 = ☐
Checks that the answer makes sense
diagnostic.language: If the student draws the story correctly but cannot tell it, the barrier is language. Let the student act it out with counters before writing, then give the frame First there were ___. Then ___.

extension.task: Write your own story for 7 + 5 = 12. Then change it into a take-away story that uses the same three numbers.
extension.reasoning: Explain how the same three numbers can fit a story that joins and a story that takes away.

en.learning: Your child is learning to solve number stories by picturing what is happening before choosing to add or subtract.
en.say: Tell the story in your own words. Is the group getting bigger or smaller?
en.ask: What happened first? What happened next? What do we need to find?
en.activity: Make up a short story with toys or snacks, like 9 grapes and 4 are eaten. Act it out, then say the number sentence together.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a resolver cuentos con números imaginando lo que pasa antes de elegir si sumar o restar.
es.say: Cuenten la historia con sus propias palabras. ¿El grupo se hace más grande o más pequeño?
es.ask: ¿Qué pasó primero? ¿Qué pasó después? ¿Qué necesitamos encontrar?
es.activity: Inventen un cuento corto con juguetes o meriendas, como 9 uvas y se comen 4. Represéntenlo y luego digan juntos la oración numérica.

skills.objective: Students add within 20 by using strategies built on facts they know: making a ten by breaking apart one addend, using doubles, and using near doubles.
skills.studentObjective: I can use a ten or a double to add numbers quickly and tell how I did it.
skills.languageObjective: I will explain my adding strategy using the words make ten, break apart, doubles and strategy.
successCriteria: I tell how many more a number needs to make ten.
I break apart the other number and add the rest to ten.
I use a double or a near double to solve a fact.
I explain my strategy in a full sentence and check it a second way.
skills.bigIdea: You can use facts you already know, like a ten or a double, to solve a harder addition fact.

syntax: I made ten with ___ and ___, then I added ___.
This is a near double because ___ is one more than ___.
discourse: Explain to a partner which strategy you chose and why

domains.listening: Students listen to a child explain a strategy and say which number was broken apart.
domains.speaking: Students tell a partner how they solved a fact and compare it with the partner's strategy.
domains.reading: Students read a short jump rope story and underline each strategy step.
domains.writing: Students write the steps of a strategy and a sentence that explains why it works.

vocab.def: Use part of one number to make 10 with the other.
vocab.example: For 8 + 5, take 2 from the 5 to make 10 with the 8.
vocab.nonExample: Counting on from 8 one at a time
vocab.sentence: Zara uses make ten to solve 8 + 5.

vocab.def: To split a number into two smaller numbers.
vocab.example: Break apart 5 into 2 and 3.
vocab.nonExample: Putting 2 and 3 together to make 5
vocab.sentence: She will break apart 5 into 2 and 3.

vocab.def: Adding a number to itself, like 6 + 6.
vocab.example: 7 + 7 = 14 is a doubles fact.
vocab.nonExample: 7 + 8, which has two different numbers
vocab.sentence: Doubles facts add the same number two times.
vocab.everyday: Two of the same thing, like a double scoop of ice cream.

vocab.def: A fact next to a double, like 6 + 7.
vocab.example: 6 + 7 is one more than 6 + 6.
vocab.nonExample: 6 + 6, which is a double
vocab.sentence: A near doubles fact is one more or one less than a double.

vocab.def: A plan that helps you solve a problem.
vocab.example: Making a ten is a strategy for adding.
vocab.nonExample: Picking a number without thinking
vocab.sentence: Their teacher says that a strategy is a plan that makes adding easier.

misconceptions.belief: To make ten with 8, I need 3 more.
misconceptions.why: Students count the numbers 9, 10, 11 as three steps, or they misremember a ten bond.
misconceptions.fix: Put 8 counters in a ten frame and count the empty spaces. Say '8 and 2 make ten.'

errorCase.story: Priya wants to make ten to solve 8 + 5.
steps: Priya says 8 needs 3 more to make ten.
She breaks apart 5 into 3 and 2.
She says 8 + 3 = 10, then 10 + 2 = 12.
errorCase.explain: 8 needs 2 more to make ten, not 3. Break apart 5 into 2 and 3: 8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13.

misconceptions.belief: A near double is two more than the double.
misconceptions.why: Students see that the second number changed and add the wrong amount to the double.
misconceptions.fix: Build 6 + 6 with counters and add exactly one more counter for 6 + 7.

errorCase.story: Tomás knows 6 + 6 = 12 and wants to solve 6 + 7.
steps: 7 is one more than 6, so Tomás adds 2 more to 12.
He says 6 + 7 = 14.
errorCase.explain: 7 is only one more than 6, so the answer is one more than 12. 6 + 7 = 13.

misconceptions.belief: 'Double 5' means 5 and 2, so 5 + 2.
misconceptions.why: In everyday talk, double sounds like 'two', so students add the number 2 instead of a second copy.
misconceptions.fix: Say 'two groups of 5' and show two hands with 5 fingers each. Write 5 + 5 = 10.

misconceptions.belief: Each addition fact can be solved with only one strategy.
misconceptions.why: Students think the strategy belongs to the fact instead of to the person solving it.
misconceptions.fix: Solve 7 + 8 as a near double and as a make ten, and show that both give 15.

reading.title: The Jump Rope Team
reading.text: Zara and Kofi count jump rope turns at recess. Zara jumps 8 times, and Kofi jumps 5 times. Zara wants to add 8 + 5. She uses make ten. She says 8 needs 2 more to make ten. She breaks apart 5 into 2 and 3. Then 8 + 2 = 10 and 10 + 3 = 13. Kofi uses doubles. He knows 6 + 6 = 12, and he wants 6 + 7. A near double is one more than a double, so 6 + 7 is 13. Their teacher says that a strategy is a plan that makes adding easier.
reading.simple: Zara and Kofi count jump rope turns. Zara jumps 8 times. Kofi jumps 5 times. Zara uses make ten for 8 + 5. She breaks apart 5 into 2 and 3. Then 8 + 2 = 10 and 10 + 3 = 13. Kofi uses doubles. He knows 6 + 6 = 12. So 6 + 7 is 13. A strategy is a plan that makes adding easier.

questions.q: How many times does Zara jump?
Why does Zara break apart 5 into 2 and 3?
questions.a: She needs 2 to make ten with 8, and the other 3 is left to add.

questions.q: What is 6 + 7?

wdntb.why: 6 + 6, 7 + 7 and 8 + 8 are doubles. 8 + 9 has two different numbers, so it is a near double.

noticeWonder.prompt: Look at 9 + 5 = 14 and 10 + 4 = 14. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

asn.claim: A doubles fact adds the same number two times.
asn.why: That is what makes it a double, like 6 + 6 or 9 + 9.

asn.claim: The make-ten strategy only works when one of the numbers is 9.
asn.why: You can make ten with 8 + 5 by breaking apart the 5 into 2 and 3, and with many other facts.

wyr.q: Would you rather solve 8 + 6 with make ten or with the double 7 + 7?

compare.a: Mei solves 9 + 6 by making ten: 9 + 1 = 10 and 10 + 5 = 15.
compare.b: Ben solves 9 + 6 by thinking 6 + 6 = 12 and then adding 3 more.
compare.prompt: Do both ways work? Which way would you pick, and why?

debate.claim: Make ten is the best strategy for adding.
debate.forEvidence: Ten is easy to work with, so after you make ten, adding the rest is quick, like 10 + 3.
debate.againstEvidence: Doubles can be faster when the two numbers are close, like 7 + 8, so make ten is not always best.

listening.script: Listen to Priya solve 9 + 4. I use make ten. 9 needs 1 more to make ten. So I break apart 4 into 1 and 3. 9 plus 1 is 10. Then 10 plus 3 is 13. So 9 + 4 is 13. My friend says 9 needs 2 more to make ten. She breaks apart 4 into 2 and 2. But 9 plus 2 is 11, not 10. A ten needs only 1 more from 9.

tasks.q: What is 9 + 4?
The friend says 9 needs 2 more to make ten. What is the error?
options: 9 needs only 1 more to make ten.
tasks.why: 9 + 1 = 10, so 9 needs only 1 more.

story.title: Recess Game Scores
story.goal: add the team scores quickly with strategies
story.intro: Elena keeps score at the recess field, and she wants to add the points fast by using a ten or a double instead of counting one by one.

beats.lead: Elena sees two scores that are close to ten.
beats.success: Elena makes a ten with one score and adds the rest, so the total is quick.
beats.redirect: The ten does not fit, so Elena counts how many more the first number really needs.

beats.lead: Two teams score almost the same number of points.
beats.success: Elena uses a double and then adds or takes one, so the total is quick.
beats.redirect: Elena adds the wrong amount to the double, so she builds the near double with counters.

beats.lead: A friend asks Elena to solve the same score a different way.
beats.success: Elena shows a second strategy and gets the same total.
beats.redirect: The two totals do not match, so Elena checks each step of both strategies.

story.ending: The scoreboard is filled in, and Elena can explain which strategy she chose and why.

panels.says: I need 7 + 8. I know that 7 + 7 is 14.
8 is one more than 7, so what is 7 + 8?
One more than 14 is 15, so 7 + 8 is 15.
I also got 15 when I made ten with the 7 and 3 from the 8.

predict.q: Samir uses a near double to solve 6 + 7. Before he says it, predict the answer.
predict.why: 6 + 6 = 12, and 7 is one more than 6, so the answer is one more than 12, which is 13.

transfer.relationship: Use a fact you know, like a ten or a double, to find a new sum
phrasings: 8 + 5: make ten with 8 and 2, then add 3
Think of 8 + 2 + 3

decoys.why: 5 was broken apart into 2 and 2, which only makes 4. It should be 2 and 3.

decoys.text: 8 + 5 is a double because both numbers are close
decoys.why: A double adds the same number twice, like 8 + 8.

modeling.title: A jump rope contest
modeling.scenario: A fictional class keeps score in a jump rope game. In round one, Team Red jumps 9 times and Team Blue jumps 7 times.
assumptions: Every jump is counted one time.
A jump counts only when the rope goes under both feet.
The numbers are invented for this exercise.
prompts: Use make ten or doubles to find how many jumps Team Red and Team Blue made together in round one.
Team Red jumps 6 more times in round two. How many jumps does Team Red have in all?
Which strategy did you choose, and why?
limits: Different people may choose different strategies, and each can be right.
A real game can have mistakes if someone counts a jump twice.

sentence.but: 8 + 5 is not a double, but a ten can still help.
sentence.so: 8 needs 2 to make ten, so I break apart 5 into 2 and 3.

diagnostic.prompt: Ask the student to solve 9 + 6. Say: Show me a way that uses a ten or a double. Then ask for a second way.
lookFor: Finds how many the first number needs to make ten
Breaks apart the other number correctly
Gets the same total with a second strategy
diagnostic.language: If the student can fill a ten frame correctly but cannot say what they did, the barrier is language. Offer the frame: I made ten with ___ and ___.

extension.task: Solve 8 + 7 in two different ways: with make ten and with a near double. Show the steps of both.
extension.reasoning: Explain why both ways give the same answer.

en.learning: Your child is learning to add by using facts that are easy to know, like making a ten or using a double.
en.say: Use a ten to help. If you have 8 and need 10, how many more is that?
en.ask: How did you add it? Is there another way to get the same answer?
en.activity: Put 8 buttons in one cup and 5 in another. Move buttons until one cup has 10, then say how many are in all.

es.learning: Su hijo o hija está aprendiendo a sumar con datos fáciles de recordar, como formar una decena o usar dobles.
es.say: Usen una decena para ayudarse. Si tienen 8 y necesitan 10, ¿cuántos más son?
es.ask: ¿Cómo lo sumaste? ¿Hay otra manera de llegar a la misma respuesta?
es.activity: Pongan 8 botones en una taza y 5 en otra. Muevan botones hasta que una taza tenga 10 y digan cuántos hay en total.
